title: Computational imaging — Computational photography, light field and coded aperture
text:
Plenoptic photography — Light Field Theory

Motivations
A classic photograph only captures a 2D projection of the scene: it loses almost all of the directional information of the light.
A plenoptic camera (light field camera) records how light varies not only in spatial position, but also in direction. It captures the vectors of light rays: where they come from, and how they are manipulated by the lenses.






NoteTo remember



An ordinary photograph responds to: what intensity of light arrives at this point on the sensor? A plenoptic camera responds to: what intensity of light arrives at this point, coming from this direction? This additional directional information is what makes refocusing and changing point of view possible after capture.




The Plenoptic Function
The light field can be defined as the geometric distribution of light rays circulating in space.
The most general representation is the 5D plenoptic function:
\[L(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)\]
Or :

\((x, y, z)\) — spatial position of the observation point (3 dimensions)
\(\theta\) — polar angle of the direction of the ray
\(\phi\) — azimuthal angle of the direction of the ray







TipIntuition



Imagine yourself standing in a room. For each point where you could stand \((x,y,z)\) and each direction where you could look \((\theta, \phi)\), the plenoptic function gives the brightness you would perceive. It is an exhaustive and total description of all the light in the scene — an “infinite catalog” of rays.




Radiance and light field
Physically, the value of the plenoptic function corresponds to the radiance (energy luminance) at a given point and in a given direction. In free space (without diffusion or absorption), the radiance of a ray remains constant along its trajectory.
This conservation property makes it possible to reduce the description of 5D to 4D: a ray is entirely defined by its intersection with two parallel planes — this is the two-plane parametrization, denoted \((s, t, u, v)\):

st plane — the first plane (for example, the lens plane)
uv plane — the second plane (for example, the plane of the sensor or an output window)



Measuring rays with a pinhole camera
A pinhole camera placed at a point measures all the rays passing through that point — it’s a sample of the light field. By moving the same pinhole camera successively to several positions, the complete light field is reconstructed.
The same set of rays can be captured by:

A single pinhole camera moved to multiple points of view.
Several cameras arranged in a network, taking their images simultaneously.

title: Computational imaging — Computational photography, light field and coded aperture
section: How to capture a light field?
text:
How to capture a light field?
There are three main approaches to capturing a light field.

Option 1 — Multiple Camera Network
Use a large number of cameras positioned on a 2D grid.
Iconic example: the Stanford Camera Array, comprising dozens to several hundred cameras arranged in a tight array. This system is also called Synthetic Aperture because the entire network behaves like a very large single lens.

Advantage: simultaneous capture → no motion blur.
Disadvantage: very expensive, bulky and difficult to synchronize and calibrate.

Reference: [Willburn et al., SIGGRAPH 2005]
Biological analogy: The compound eye of insects (like the mosquito) is the biological analog of a camera array: each ommatidium captures a slightly different direction of ambient light.


Option 2 — Single camera, multiple shots
Move a single camera successively to several positions using a motor.
Example: a camera mounted on a LEGO motor which moves it horizontally according to a grid.

Advantage: inexpensive.
Disadvantage: Requires a completely static scene between shots.



Option 3 — Plenoptic Camera
Insert a microlens array (microlens array, MLA) between the main lens and the photosensitive sensor, to simultaneously capture angular and spatial information in a single shot.






NoteTo remember



The term plenoptic comes from the Latin plenus (full, whole) and the Greek optikos (relating to sight). It designates a “full” vision capturing all the light information available in a single acquisition.


Historical origin: This concept was conceptualized by Gabriel Lippmann in 1908, who called it integral photography. The article describing the principle appeared in Scientific American on August 19, 1911 — more than a century ago. Practical implementation only became possible thanks to modern digital sensors.

title: Computational imaging — Computational photography, light field and coded aperture
text:
Architecture of a plenoptic camera

Conventional camera vs plenoptic camera
Conventional camera:

Subject → main lens (main lens) → sensor (photosensor)
Each pixel integrates all the rays arriving from the main objective without discriminating their angle of incidence.

Plenoptic camera:

Subject → main objective → microlens array → sensor
Each micro-lens projects a small image from the lens diaphragm onto the group of pixels in the sensor behind it.
Each group of pixels encodes the angular direction of the rays arriving at this point in image space.







TipIntuition



In a conventional camera, each pixel responds to from which point in the scene is this light coming? In a plenoptic camera, each group of pixels under a micro-lens responds to from which direction of the main lens is this light coming from? We deliberately trade a fraction of spatial resolution for angular resolution — this is the fundamental trade-off of plenoptic photography.




ST-UV setting in the plenoptic camera
In the context of the plenoptic camera, the two-plane configuration translates concretely into:

St plane — plane of the main lens (where each micro-lens is placed)
UV plane — sensor plane (the pixels behind each micro-lens encode the angular \(u,v\) coordinates)

A ray is entirely characterized by the micro-lens through which it passes (st coordinates) and the specific pixel under that micro-lens (uv coordinates).

title: Computational imaging — Computational photography, light field and coded aperture
section: Digital rendering from a light field
text:
Digital rendering from a light field
Once the light field has been captured, all subsequent operations can be carried out digitally, after the shot.

Digitally Stopping Down the Aperture
Reducing the aperture digitally consists of only summing the central portion of the pixels of each micro-lens:
\[\text{Stopping down} = \text{sommer seulement la portion centrale de chaque micro-lentille}\]

Large aperture → sum all the pixels of the micro-lens → shallow depth of field, strong bokeh.
Small aperture → only sum the central pixels → large depth of field, sharp.







TipIntuition



This is the digital equivalent of closing the aperture of a physical lens. The central pixels of the microlens correspond to the rays that pass through the center of the aperture (low angle of incidence) — exactly those that a closed diaphragm would let through.




Digitally Moving the Observer
Moving the point of view corresponds to shifting the extraction window of the pixels under each micro-lens:
\[\text{Déplacement du point de vue} = \text{décaler la fenêtre extraite de chaque micro-lentille}\]
By systematically extracting the left (or right, or top, etc.) pixels from each micro-lens, we synthesize an image seen from a slightly different angle — thus creating a digital parallax.


Digital Refocusing
Digital refocusing is the most spectacular operation: freely choose the sharpness plane after shooting.
\[\text{Refocalisation} = \text{sommer des fenêtres décalées extraites de plusieurs micro-lentilles}\]
By summing sub-windows extracted from neighboring micro-lenses with a calculated offset, we simulate the digital movement of the sensor plane — which corresponds to changing the focus.






ImportantKey principle



Digital refocusing is a digital integration of light rays: by accumulating the contributions of several micro-lenses with the correct offsets, we reconstruct the image that would have been produced by a sensor placed at a different distance from the lens. It is a synthesis of the focus entirely made after capture.


Illustration of the result:

A single image captured with the plenoptic camera can be refocused on near or distant objects.
You can also produce a “clean” image by combining refocuses at different depths — like a focal stack extracted from a single capture.

title: Computational imaging — Computational photography, light field and coded aperture
text:
The Lytro Camera

General presentation
The Lytro camera is the first commercial realization of a consumer plenoptic camera. It concretely embodies the theoretical principles of the light field.
Two models exist:

Lytro — compact and portable model (form factor: rectangular parallelepiped)
Lytro Illum Pro — professional version with interchangeable lens and higher resolution



Internal architecture
The Lytro camera integrates four main components:

Lens Array — the micro-lens array placed directly in front of the sensor
Light Field Sensor (Light Field Sensor) — the CMOS sensor augmented with micro-lenses
Light Field Engine (Light Field Engine) — the dedicated signal processor for plenoptic processing
Marvell Avastar 88W8787 SoC — integrated chip providing WiFi and Bluetooth capabilities for data transfer



The light field sensor (Light Field Sensor)
The sensor combines two complementary technologies:
CMOS sensor:

Standard technology of modern digital cameras.
Converts light into electrical charges stored in cells, read and converted to digital values.
Sensitive, fast and inexpensive.

Micro lens array:

Attached directly to the CMOS sensor surface.
Divides the sensor pixels into groups, with each group corresponding to a micro-lens.
Each micro-lens projects an image of the main lens aperture onto its associated pixels.
The result: each pixel of the sensor encodes not only where the light arrives on the sensor, but also from what angular direction it comes.







TipIntuition



We can visualize the micro-lens array as a “ray sorter”: instead of each pixel receiving light directly from the scene via the main lens, it receives it via a small intermediate lens which directs a precise direction from the lens towards it. Each micro-lens is like a small “directional window”.




Advantages and disadvantages of the Lytro camera








Appearance
Advantage
Disadvantage




Portability
Highly portable, compact size
—


Post-capture flexibility
Digital refocusing after shooting
—


Full resolution
—
Reduced effective resolution (spatial/angular trade-off)


Opening
—
Fixed aperture (no physical control of depth of field)









ImportantFundamental Resolution Tradeoff



The total resolution of the sensor is shared between spatial resolution and angular resolution. The more angles we want (more different views) per point in the scene, the fewer pixels we have per view. A plenoptic camera always has a lower effective spatial resolution than a conventional camera with the same sensor.

title: Computational imaging — Computational photography, light field and coded aperture
text:
Conventional camera with coded aperture

Objective and motivations
The objective of this section is to show how a minor modification of the lens — replacing the standard circular aperture with a binary mask (coded aperture) — makes it possible to extract from a single image:

A depth map — the distances of objects in the scene
An all-focused image — digitally deconvolved







TipIntuition



A coded aperture transforms defocus blur into an informative and identifiable signal. Instead of an ambiguous circular blur, we get a blur bearing the mask’s distinctive signature — unique enough to be numerically identified (giving depth) and inverted (giving the sharp image).




Lens, defocus and point spread function (PSF)

Perfect focus
When an object is exactly on the focal plane:

All rays coming from a point on the object converge towards a single pixel of the sensor.
The PSF (Point Spread Function) is an ideal point, very concentrated.



Defocus (object out of focal plane)
When an object is out of the focal plane (either in front or behind):

Rays coming from a point no longer converge on a single pixel.
They form a circle of confusion on the sensor.
The PSF is no longer a point but an extended spot whose shape resembles that of the aperture of the lens.







NoteTo remember



The PSF describes how a source point is spread across the sensor. For a conventional defocus camera, the PSF is a scaled version of the aperture shape (pentagon, hexagon or circle depending on the aperture). The size of the PSF increases with distance from the focal plane — and therefore reveals depth.


The size of the PSF is directly related to depth: the farther the object is from the focal plane, the larger the PSF. This is the basis of depth inference by defocusing.



Model: defocus as local convolution
In a defocused image, each local region can be modeled as a local convolution:
\[y' = f_k \otimes x\]
Or :

\(y'\) — local subwindow of the observed defocused image
\(x\) — corresponding sub-window of the sharp image (unknown)
\(f_k\) — blur kernel calibrated to depth \(k\) (PSF at this depth)
\(\otimes\) — 2D convolution operator







TipIntuition



Each depth \(k\) corresponds to a PSF \(f_k\) of different size. The inference problem consists of finding, for each region of the image, which PSF \(f_k\) produced the observed blur — and therefore what is the depth \(k\) of this region. This is a model selection problem.


Numerical examples:

Depth \(k=1\) (near object) → PSF large, circle of confusion wide
Depth \(k=2\) (object at intermediate distance) → average PSF
Depth \(k=3\) (distant object, close to the focal plane) → PSF small, almost a point

Algorithm overview:

Try to deconvolute the local window with each calibrated filter \(f_k\).
Select the scale that gives the most “natural” result.
The estimated depth is that corresponding to this scale.



Challenges of the conventional approach
Two major problems prevent this approach from working directly with a standard circular aperture:

Challenge 1 — Discriminate defocus blur from a smooth scene
A uniformly colored region of the scene may look like a heavily defocused region. It is difficult to distinguish depth blur from inherently smooth content of the scene.
Example: A slightly defocused white wall produces the same observation as a perfectly sharp white wall — in both cases, a uniform area without texture.


Challenge 2 — Reversing defocus blur is an ill-posed problem
Deconvolution is an ill-posed problem. Formally:
\[f \otimes x = y\]
For a given PSF \(f\) and an observed image \(y\), there exists an infinity of solutions \(x\) satisfying this equation. Two solutions with the same convolution can look like very different images. Especially :

Classic algorithms like Richardson-Lucy introduce ringing artifacts — parasitic oscillations at the contours of objects.
The standard circular PSF has zero frequencies in its spectrum → some spatial frequencies are completely lost → impossible to reconstruct them.




Proposed solutions

Solution 1 — Natural Images Prior
Natural images have a distinctive statistical property: their gradients are sparse.

A natural image has mainly uniform areas with sharp edges → non-zero gradient only at the edges (sparse distribution).
An unnatural image (noise, ringing artifacts) has dense gradients everywhere (non-sparse distribution).

We incorporate this knowledge into the deconvolution via a regularization term:
\[x = \arg\min_x \left\| f \otimes x - y \right\|^2 + \lambda \sum_i \rho(\nabla x_i)\]
Or :

\(\|f \otimes x - y\|^2\) — data attachment term: the reconstructed image convolved with the PSF must give the observed image
\(\lambda \sum_i \rho(\nabla x_i)\) — regularization term: penalizes large gradients to favor natural images
\(\lambda\) — balance parameter between the two terms

Choice of function \(\rho\):

\(\rho(\nabla x) = \|\nabla x\|^2\) — Gaussian prior (“spread” gradients): favors weak gradients everywhere, gives a smooth result, not favorable to sharp edges.
\(\rho(\nabla x) = \|\nabla x\|^{0.8}\) — sparse priori (“localizes” gradients): concentrates the gradients at the edges, gives a result with sharp contours and flat areas.

The experimental comparison clearly shows that the sparse prior significantly outperforms Richardson-Lucy and the Gaussian prior for edge restoration.






TipIntuition



The sparse prior says: “a good natural image should have few gradients, concentrated at the edges of objects”. By minimizing the total energy (data fidelity + gradient penalty), we guide the deconvolution towards a solution that looks like a real photo rather than a noisy or oscillating signal.




Solution 2 — Coded Aperture
Rather than acting only on the calculation, we physically modify the optical system: we insert a pseudo-random binary mask (occluder) in the plane of the aperture of the objective.
Effect on PSF:

With a classic aperture (smooth circle or polygon) → smooth PSF, difficult to distinguish from a naturally blurred scene.
With a coded aperture (pseudo-random binary pattern) → PSF bearing the characteristic signature of the mask → easily identifiable and discriminable from the natural content of the scene.







NoteTo remember



Coded aperture transforms the defocus PSF into a unique identifier. Each depth produces a scaled version of that pattern — scale reveals depth, and the presence of the pattern unambiguously distinguishes defocus from a naturally smooth scene.


Consequence on depth estimation: Since the encoded PSF is distinct from the natural content of the images, it becomes possible to identify the depth even in poorly textured areas.



Zero Frequencies — Design Compromise (Zero Frequencies Trade-off)
The shape of the coded aperture mask determines the frequency spectrum of the PSF. A key design choice concerns zero frequencies (spectral zeros):
Mask without zero frequencies:

✅ The filter can be easily inverted (zero-free spectrum → stable division in Fourier space)
❌ Weaker depth discrimination (less distinctive PSF)

Mask with zero frequencies:

✅ Spectral zeros improve depth discrimination (very distinctive PSF)
❌ Difficult inversion (division by zero in the frequency domain → numerical instability)
✅ Inversion is made possible thanks to the priori on natural images: even if certain frequencies are lost, the priori guides the reconstruction







ImportantKey principle



The optimal coded aperture is designed so that its PSF is maximally discriminable from the natural content of the images. Using a prior on natural images allows zero frequencies to be accepted in the PSF — which improves depth discrimination without sacrificing deconvolution quality. The two ideas (priori + coded opening) are complementary.




Results and results of coded opening
Qualitative results observed:

From a single defocused image captured with the coded aperture, the algorithm produces:

A colorimetric depth map (red = near, blue = far)
A clear image (all-focus) after deconvolution with the correct estimated kernel


Advantages/disadvantages balance sheet:








Appearance
Advantage
Disadvantage




Entrance
Image AND depth from single take
—


Spatial resolution
No loss of spatial resolution
—


Hardware modification
Minimal lens modification
—


Depth accuracy
—
Coarse depth, impossible in textureless areas


Light
Deconvolution increases effective depth of field
Slight loss of light (mask blocks some rays)

title: Computational imaging — Computational photography, light field and coded aperture
text:
Camera with Generalized Optics

General principle
Previous systems modified the aperture (coded aperture). A more radical approach is to change the optics themselves — the shape or arrangement of the lenses.
The main idea is: change the optics, not just the aperture (change optics, not aperture).
The objective is to design a PSF which, combined with appropriate digital processing, makes it possible to obtain both a clear image and a depth map from a single acquisition.


Wavefront Coding
Wavefront coding modifies the surface of a lens in such a way as to introduce a controlled aberration (typically a cubic phase) that makes the PSF approximately depth invariant over a certain range of distances.
Standard lens vs. wavefront encoded lens comparison:

Standard lens:

Exact focus → PSF = ideal point, very sharp
Out of focus → PSF = extended spot very different depending on depth

Wavefront encoded lens:

In-focus AND out-of-focus → PSF ≈ the same spread shape (approximately depth-invariant)
The rays no longer converge towards a single point but disperse in a controlled and reproducible manner


Digital processing:
Since the PSF is approximately the same for all depths, a single global deconvolution with this single PSF restores sharpness across the entire scene. No need to estimate depth locally.






TipIntuition



The wavefront encoded lens acts as a “uniform blur”: everything is slightly blurred in the same way, regardless of depth. A single deconvolution restores all sharpness. This is advantageous when you want a large depth of field without estimating a depth map.




Lattice Lens
The lattice lens (lattice lens) adds an array of lenslets (small lenses) with variable focal length in front of the main lens.
Architecture :

2D array of variable focal length micro-lenses → arranged in front of the main lens
Each micro-lens deflects the rays slightly differently depending on its position
Result: the PSF varies according to the depth of the object → depth information encoded in the image







NoteTo remember



The array lens is conceptually similar to the microlens array of the plenoptic camera — but here the microlenses are placed in front of the main lens, not between the lens and sensor. The effect is different: we create spatially structured and depth-varying PSFs rather than separating the angles.




Spectral analysis: the dimensionality gap
The full light field is 4D (st-uv coordinates). But in an image and depth oriented application, all the useful information is found in a 3D subspace:

Light field spectrum: 4D
Image spectrum: 2D
Depth: 1D
Useful total: 3D — this is what Ng (2005) calls the dimensionality gap

Only the 3D subspace corresponding to the physical focus distance is useful. The grating lens is designed to precisely capture this subspace, ignoring the remaining 1D of the light field that does not contain relevant information for image+depth reconstruction.
Practical consequence: The grating lens is more efficient (in terms of sensor pixel usage) than the full plenoptic camera for depth-oriented applications.
Limitations:

PSF is not depth invariant → local deconvolution required, similar to coded aperture.
The PSFs at different depths have very distinct shapes → allow the depth to be estimated locally.

Reference: [Ng, 2005]

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Definition: Process of indirect image formation from raw measurements, using computation-intensive algorithms. It relies on the co-design of the acquisition system and the reconstruction algorithm (inseparable).
Pipeline:

Traditional: Optics → Recognizable image → Computation (enhancement)
Computational: Generalized optics → Coded representation → Generalized computation → Final images

Two fundamental steps:

Optical encoding — new optics, sensors, light sources
Computational recovery — new decoding/reconstruction algorithms

Three disciplinary pillars: Mathematics (optimization, ML) · Physics (optics) · Computation (algorithms)
Mathematical formalism: \[y = Ax + n\]

\(y\): raw measurements, \(A\): measurement operator (physics), \(x\): unknown image, \(n\): noise
Ill-posed problem (Hadamard) → requires regularization (prior on \(x\))

Key difference vs classical image processing: computation does not only enhance — it decodes a representation that is not directly readable.
Biological analogy: mantis shrimp (16 photoreceptor types) — sensor and brain are inseparable.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Base constraint: smartphones = tiny sensors with limited optics → quality comes from algorithms, not from optics.
Key opto-algorithmic co-design techniques:

HDR — Capture \(N\) exposures (under/normal/over) → align + merge + tone mapping to cover up to 14 orders of magnitude of dynamic range
Night mode / Burst — ~15 short images → sub-pixel alignment → temporal fusion (accumulate light without motion blur)
Multi-sensors — Fuse wide + standard + tele + ToF → super-resolution, synthetic bokeh, variable depth-of-field in post
Coded aperture — Binary mask in the diaphragm → extract depth + all-in-focus image from a single shot
Focal stack — Fuse images focused at different distances → global sharpness across the scene
Hyperspectral imaging — Dozens to hundreds of spectral bands → identify materials/vegetation/pollutants

Unifying principle: optics encodes → algorithm decodes. The two are co-designed and inseparable.

text:
Summary
Definition: end-to-end (end-to-end) co-optimization of physical optics and a neural network for a final task.
Two-layer architecture:

Physical layer — lens / coded mask / diffractive element / freeform phase surface, parameterized in a differentiable way
Digital layer — neural network decoder

Training phase:

Differentiable simulation of image formation (physics model)
Loss gradient backpropagated through the network and through the optical simulation
Lens parameters (surface heights, phase) optimized simultaneously with network weights via SGD

Inference phase:

Optimized lens manufactured physically (micro-fabrication, 3D printing)
Trained network deployed alongside
Both layers run together on real data

Two interpretations:

Optical encoder + electronic decoder
Hybrid optical–electronic neural network (physical layer = first layers)

Key principle: optics no longer needs to output a “pretty” image — it must encode the useful information optimally for the target task. Highly aberrated lenses can outperform “perfect” lenses for some tasks.
Applications: extended depth-of-field, 3D from a single image, gaze-contingent displays, direct classification.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Definition: reconstruct an object hidden behind an obstacle by exploiting light bounces on diffuse surfaces.
Physical principle — the 3rd bounce: \[\text{Laser} \to \text{visible wall} \to \text{hidden object} \to \text{visible wall} \to \text{sensor}\] The time difference between the 1st bounce (direct) and the 3rd bounce encodes the 3D position of the hidden object.
Experimental setup:







Component
Role




Picosecond laser
Ultra-short pulses (\(\sim 10^{-12}\) s) for time resolution


2-axis galvanometer mirror
Scan the laser over many wall points


Beamsplitter
Separates emission and return to avoid saturation


SPAD sensor
Single-photon detector, ~ps time resolution


Occluder
Hides the object to isolate the 3rd-bounce signal



Acquired data: 3D volume \((x', y', t)\) — not directly interpretable.
Reconstruction: algorithms inspired by filtered back-projection (CT) or Phasor Fields (treat as spatio-temporal wavefield propagation).
Main challenge: the useful signal (3rd bounce) is 10–100× weaker than the direct signal → fast deconvolution or compressed-sensing-like methods required.
Applications: autonomous driving (see around a corner) · rescue (locate behind a wall) · medical endoscopy.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary







Parameter
Key value




Visual acuity
~1 arcminute, 20/20 — maximum in fovea (~180 × 10³ cones/mm²)


Field of view
200° horizontal (120° binocular + 40° monocular each side), 135° vertical


Temporal resolution
~60 Hz (below → flicker perceived)


Dynamic range
5 orders (instantaneous) — 14 orders / 46.5 f-stops (adapted)


Color vision
3 cone types: S/M/L — perceptually linear space: CIE Lab


Spectral sensitivity
S cones: 419 nm · M: 531 nm · L: 559 nm · Rods: 496 nm


Accommodation
8 cm–∞ at age 16 → 50 cm–∞ at age 50 (presbyopia = lens stiffening)


CSF
Peak at 4–6 cpd, limit ~60 cpd, low-frequency falloff (lateral inhibition)


Depth perception
Stereopsis (vergence + binocular disparity) + monocular cues (accommodation + retinal blur)



Important notes:

The eye’s superior dynamic range motivates HDR techniques
The CSF explains the acceptability of JPEG compression (removing high frequencies)
Binocular vision (~120° central) is crucial for stereopsis

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Eye diameter: ~24 mm. Optical pipeline: cornea + lens (lenses) · iris (aperture stop) · retina (sensor).
Anterior structures:








Element
Role
Key detail




Cornea
~70% of refraction
Fixed curvature, does not accommodate


Iris
Diaphragm
Smooth muscles → pupil 2–8 mm depending on light


Anterior chamber
Cornea–iris space
Filled with aqueous humour (nourishes cornea + lens)



Lens — accommodation element:

~30% of refractive power
Ciliary muscles contracted → zonules relaxed → lens rounder (near vision)
Ciliary muscles relaxed → zonules taut → lens flatter (far vision)
Stiffens with age → presbyopia

Posterior structures:







Element
Role




Vitreous body
Gel (99% water), maintains shape


Retina
Photosensitive sensor (photoreceptors)


Fovea
Center of retina, ~1–2 mm, maximum cone density, high resolution


Optic disc
Optic nerve exit — blind spot (no photoreceptors)


Choroid
Vascular supply to outer retina


Sclera
External protection (white layer)



Inverted organization: light crosses ganglion + bipolar neurons before reaching photoreceptors.
Refractive errors:

Emmetropia: focus on retina (normal)
Myopia: focus before retina → concave lens
Hypermetropia: focus behind retina → convex lens
Astigmatism: irregular curvature → no single focus → cylindrical lens

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Three-layer structure (inner → outer):

Retinal ganglion cells (RGC) — output neurons → optic nerve
Collector cells — bipolar (relay) + horizontal (lateral integration) + amacrine (modulation)
Receptor cells — photoreceptors (rods + cones)


Note: inverted organization — light crosses layers 1 and 2 before reaching layer 3.

Rods — scotopic system:

~10⁸; extreme sensitivity (respond to 1 photon via phototransduction cascade × 10⁶)
Strong convergence → low resolution, no color, peak at 496 nm
Absent from fovea; maximum at 15–20° eccentricity

Cones — photopic system:

~10⁷; require high luminance
Near 1-to-1 wiring in fovea → high resolution
3 types: S (419 nm) · M (531 nm) · L (559 nm)

Retinal ganglion cells (RGC):

Encode luminance differences (not absolute levels)
Center-surround organization: on-center and off-center
Two classes: M (magnocellular — motion, temporal) and P (parvocellular — color, spatial detail)

Spatial distribution:

Fovea: maximum cones, high resolution
Periphery: dominated by rods (max at 15–20°) → look slightly aside to see a faint star
Blind spot: optic disc, no photoreceptors

Optic nerve bandwidth: insufficient to transmit all raw signals → visual encoding begins in the retina.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Visual pathway to V1: \[\text{Retina} \to \text{Optic nerve} \to \text{Optic chiasm} \to \text{LGN} \to \text{V1}\]

Optic chiasm: nasal fibers cross → left visual field processed by right hemisphere (and vice versa)
LGN: 2 magnocellular layers (M cells) + 4 parvocellular layers (P cells) — retinotopic organization preserved

Three types of cells in V1 (Hubel & Wiesel, Nobel 1981):








Type
Receptive field
Function




Center-surround
Circular antagonistic
Continuation of retinal processing


Simple cells
Elongated, fixed position
Oriented edge detectors at a specific position/orientation


Complex cells
Elongated, position-tolerant
Orientation-selective, but less sensitive to exact location



Hypercolumns: V1 organization encoding simultaneously:

Eye-of-origin (left/right) → ocular dominance columns
Preferred orientation → orientation columns
Retinotopic location → global organization


Hebb’s rule: neurons that fire together wire together

CSF: reflects frequency filtering properties of V1 (peak 4–6 cpd, limit ~60 cpd, lateral inhibition at low frequencies).
Streams beyond V1:

Ventral stream (V1→V2→V4→TEO→TE): the “What” — object recognition, color, texture, identity
Dorsal stream (V1→V2→V3→MT→parietal cortex): the “Where” — location, motion

Impact on AI: Hubel & Wiesel’s discoveries → neocognitron → CNN.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Two core biological inspirations:

Orientation selectivity in V1 → SIFT and HOG descriptors (histograms of oriented gradients)
Hierarchy of the ventral stream (simple → complex → hypercomplex) → Neocognitron → CNN

The Neocognitron (Fukushima):

Architecture: input → retina → LGN → S layers (simple) → C layers (complex) → … → “grandmother” cell
S layers ↔︎ V1 simple cells: local oriented filters, position-specific
C layers ↔︎ V1 complex cells: spatial pooling, translation invariance
First network capable of translation-invariant recognition

LeNet (LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, Haffner — 1998):
\[\text{Image (28×28)} \to \text{Conv C1 (6 filters)} \to \text{Pool S2} \to \text{Conv C3 (16 filters)} \to \text{Pool S4} \to \text{Dense F5 (120)} \to \text{Dense F6 (84)} \to \text{10 classes}\]

Convolutions = learned Gabor-like filters (good approximation of simple cells)
Pooling = invariance to small translations (analogy with complex cells)

Increasing specificity in the hierarchy:








Level
Biology (ventral stream)
CNN




Low
V1: oriented edges (Gabor)
Early layers: edges, colors


Mid
V2–V4: combinations, shapes
Intermediate layers: object parts


High
IT: faces, whole objects
Deep layers: abstract representations



Limitation of the model: feedback connections in the ventral stream (bidirectional, top-down back to V1) are absent from standard CNNs. Good visual architectures are likely hierarchical and mostly feedforward.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Conventional (decoupled) pipeline: \[\text{Real world} \to \text{Standard optics} \to \underbrace{\text{Readable image}}_{\text{already interpretable}} \to \text{Computation (enhancement)} \to \text{Final image}\]
Computational (coupled) pipeline: \[\text{Real world} \to \text{Generalized optics} \to \underbrace{\text{Coded representation}}_{\text{not readable}} \to \text{Computation (decoding)} \to \text{Multiple final outputs}\]
Comparison table:








Criterion
Conventional
Computational




Role of optics
Form a readable image
Encode information


Role of computation
Enhance an already readable image
Decode the coded representation


Co-design
Independent
Mandatory (sensor ↔︎ algorithm)


Outputs
One 2D image
Multiple (sharp image, depth, views, …)



Co-design examples:

CFA mosaic (Bayer): encodes color pixel-by-pixel → demosaicing reconstructs full RGB
Plenoptic camera: encodes ray direction (microlens array) → computation reconstructs refocused views
Coded aperture: encodes depth in blur (PSF) → computation extracts depth map + all-in-focus image

Physical trade-offs exceeded:

Large aperture ↔︎ shallow depth of field → coded aperture / focal stack
Light ↔︎ sharpness → night mode (burst photography)
Pinhole (everything sharp, little light) ↔︎ lens (efficient, limited DoF) → computation aims to combine the advantages

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Definition: series of images captured at different focus distances, fused to produce an all-in-focus image.
Analogy: as HDR extends dynamic range by combining several exposures, a focal stack extends depth of field by combining several focus settings.
Capturing the stack:

Vary \(D'\) (lens–sensor distance) via the focus ring
Or vary \(D\) (object–lens distance) via camera/object motion (macro, motorized rail StackShot)

3-step fusion:

Alignment — correct magnification changes \(m = f / (D' - f)\) via isotropic scaling
Sharpness measure — apply the Laplacian operator to each image (strong response = sharp regions) + Gaussian smoothing of weight maps
Weighted fusion — \(I_{\text{sharp}} = \dfrac{\sum_k w_k \cdot I_k}{\sum_k w_k}\) where \(w_k\) = sharpness map

Typical applications: macro photography (very small DoF) · optical microscopy (DoF ~ µm) · landscape photography.
Bonus: the focal stack also enables depth inference — the focus setting where a pixel is sharpest reveals its distance to the camera (→ Question 16).

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Common physical principle: the size and shape of the PSF (Point Spread Function) are linked to depth — on-focus → point-like PSF; off-focus → growing circle of confusion.
Four techniques compared:









Technique
Input
Output
Particularities




Confocal stereo
Focus + aperture stack (2D)
Per pixel
Very accurate, resolves depth/texture ambiguity; data-hungry [Hassinof & Kutulakos, ECCV 2006]


Depth from focus
1D focal stack
Per patch
Standard; Laplacian sharpness, depth = best-focus setting of the patch


Focal flow
Dense focal stack
Per patch
No convolution; models PSF as Gaussian (\(\sigma\) varies), measures optical flow between frames; works only in textured regions; inspired by the jumping spider [Alexander et al., ECCV 2016; Guo et al., ICCV 2017]


Depth from defocus
2 images only
Per patch
Minimal data; \(g_i = f * h_{\sigma_i}\), compare the two to extract \(\sigma\) → depth



Key trade-off: depth accuracy ↔︎ amount of required data.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Motivation: classical photography captures a 2D projection (intensity only) → ray direction lost → focus, aperture, viewpoint fixed at capture.
Light field: geometric distribution of light rays in space.
Plenoptic function:

Full version: \(L(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)\) — 5D
Reduced (free space, radiance conserved along a ray): 4D via two-plane parameterization \((s, t, u, v)\)

st plane = main lens (which microlens)
uv plane = sensor (which pixel under the microlens)


Three post-capture numerical operations:








Operation
Mechanism
Effect




Stopping down
Sum only central pixels under each microlens
Increases depth of field


Viewpoint change
Shift the pixel-extraction window
Creates numerical parallax


Digital refocusing
Sum shifted windows across neighboring microlenses
Simulates a new focal plane



Fundamental trade-off: total sensor resolution is shared between spatial and angular resolution (more views → fewer pixels per view).
Historical origin: Gabriel Lippmann (1908) — integral photography, Scientific American article of Aug 19, 1911.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Three hardware approaches:









Approach
Example
Advantage
Drawback




Camera array
Stanford Camera Array
Simultaneous capture, dynamic scenes
Expensive, complex calibration


Moving single camera
Camera on a LEGO motor
Low cost, no calibration
Requires a static scene


Plenoptic camera
Lytro
One shot, portable
Reduced spatial resolution



Biological analogy (camera array): insect compound eye — each ommatidium captures a different direction.
Plenoptic camera architecture:
\[\text{Subject} \to \text{Main lens} \to \underbrace{\text{Microlens array (MLA)}}_{\text{"ray sorter"}} \to \text{Sensor}\]
Each microlens images the aperture onto its pixel group → each pixel encodes a precise angular direction.
Lytro — first commercial realization:



Component
Role




Lens Array
MLA directly on the sensor


Light Field Sensor
CMOS + microlenses


Light Field Engine
Dedicated signal processor


Marvell Avastar 88W8787 SoC
WiFi + Bluetooth transfer



Resolution trade-off: if each microlens covers \(N \times N\) pixels → angular resolution = \(N^2\) directions, spatial resolution divided by \(N^2\) relative to a conventional camera.

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Principle: insert a pseudo-random binary mask in the aperture plane → turn the defocus PSF into a unique identifier that is discriminable from naturally smooth image content.
Basic physical model: \[y' = f_k \otimes x\] where \(y'\) = observed image, \(x\) = unknown sharp scene, \(f_k\) = PSF at depth \(k\). Estimating \(k\) means finding the \(f_k\) that best explains the observation.
Two challenges with a standard aperture:

Smooth circular PSF is indistinguishable from naturally uniform content
Deconvolution is ill-posed — zeros in the PSF spectrum → lost frequencies + ringing artifacts

Solution 1 — Prior on natural images:
Natural images have sparse gradients (flat regions + sharp edges) → regularization: \[x = \arg\min_x \left\| f \otimes x - y \right\|^2 + \lambda \sum_i \rho(\nabla x_i)\]

\(\rho(\nabla x) = \|\nabla x\|^2\) → Gaussian prior (smooth, not ideal)
\(\rho(\nabla x) = \|\nabla x\|^{0.8}\) → sparse prior (sharp edges + flat regions, better than Richardson–Lucy)

Solution 2 — Coded aperture:

Binary mask → PSF carries the mask signature → identifiable at all depths
Each depth = scaled version of the pattern → scale reveals depth
Optimal combination: mask with zero frequencies (better discrimination) + sparse prior (stabilizes deconvolution despite zeros)

Result from a single image: depth map + all-in-focus image.
Summary table:




Advantage
Limitation




Input
Single image
—


Resolution
No spatial loss
—


Hardware
Only a mask in the diaphragm
—


Depth
—
Coarse; textureless regions problematic


Light
—
Slight loss (mask blocks some rays)

title: Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging
text:
Summary
Principle: modify the lens itself (not just the aperture) to encode more information in the measurement.
Technique 1 — Wavefront coding:

Modify the lens surface to introduce a controlled cubic phase aberration
Result: PSF approximately depth-invariant over a range
Digital processing: a single global deconvolution restores sharpness over the whole scene
✅ Large effective depth of field
❌ No depth map (PSFs identical → no depth information)

Technique 2 — Lattice lens:

2D array of microlenses with varying focal lengths placed in front of the main lens

≠ plenoptic camera (MLA between lens and sensor)

PSF varies with depth → depth estimation possible
✅ Produces depth + sharp image · ✅ Exploits the dimensionality gap
❌ Requires local patch-wise deconvolution

Dimensionality gap (Ng, 2005):

Full light field: 4D
Useful information for image + depth: 3D (2D image + 1D depth)
The lattice lens captures precisely this 3D subspace → more efficient than capturing the full 4D light field when the goal is depth.

Course-wide recap table:









System
Modification
Main advantage
Limitation




Conventional
None
Simplicity
Limited depth of field


Focal stack
None (multiple shots)
Sharp image + depth
Static scene


Plenoptic camera
MLA between lens and sensor
Refocusing, multi-views
Reduced spatial resolution


Coded aperture
Mask in the diaphragm
Depth + sharp image in 1 shot
Coarse depth


Wavefront coding
Lens with cubic phase
Large depth of field
No depth map


Lattice lens
MLA in front of the lens
Efficient depth + sharpness
Local deconvolution

title: The Human Visual System — Quiz
text:
### Quel scientifique a le premier proposé que la lumière va des objets vers l’œil, et non l’inverse ?

> Pense au scientifique du Moyen Âge considéré comme le plus grand opticien de son époque.

1. [ ] Platon
    > Incorrect : Platon défendait une théorie extromissive — l’œil émettrait de la lumière.
1. [ ] Aristote
    > Incorrect : Aristote proposait des images matérielles transportées par l’atmosphère.
1. [x] Alhazen
    > Correct : Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham, 1040) renverse le paradigme en établissant que les objets envoient la lumière vers l’œil.
1. [ ] Kepler
    > Incorrect : Kepler a établi la théorie rétinienne, mais après Alhazen.


### Quelle est la fonction principale de la fovéa ?

> Pense à la zone de la rétine qui concentre le plus un certain type de photorécepteurs.

1. [ ] Detecter les faibles niveaux de lumiere
1. [x] Fournir la vision haute resolution en bonne luminosite
    > Correct : la fovéa concentre la densité maximale de cônes et est le siège de la vision fine (acuité maximale).
1. [ ] Transmettre les signaux au nerf optique
1. [ ] Controler le diametre de la pupille


### Quel est le rôle du cristallin dans l’œil humain ?

> Pense à l’élément de l’œil dont la courbure est modifiée par les muscles ciliaires.

1. [ ] Proteger l'oeil des rayons ultraviolets
1. [ ] Reguler la quantite de lumiere entrant dans l'oeil
1. [x] Ajuster la focalisation de l'image sur la retine
    > Correct : le cristallin est une lentille biconvexe dont la courbure change pour permettre l’accommodation (vision nette à différentes distances).
1. [ ] Convertir la lumiere en signaux electriques


### La résolution temporelle du système visuel humain est approximativement de :

> Pense à la fréquence minimale d’affichage pour qu’un mouvement paraisse continu à l’œil.

1. [ ] 24 Hz
1. [ ] 30 Hz
1. [x] 60 Hz
    > Correct : le système visuel humain a une résolution temporelle d’environ 60 Hz (dépendant du contraste et de la luminance).
1. [ ] 120 Hz


### Quel type de photorécepteur est responsable de la vision des couleurs ?

> Rappelle-toi la distinction entre les deux types de photorécepteurs et leurs conditions d’activation.

1. [ ] Les batonnnets (Rods)
1. [x] Les cones (Cones)
    > Correct : les cônes sont responsables de la vision des couleurs (vision photopique). Les bâtonnets ne produisent qu’une vision en niveaux de gris (vision scotopique).
1. [ ] Les cellules bipolaires
1. [ ] Les cellules ganglionnaires


### Quelles sont les affirmations correctes concernant les bâtonnets (Rods) ?

> Pense aux conditions d’utilisation et aux propriétés des bâtonnets par rapport aux cônes.

- [x] Ils sont sensibles aux faibles niveaux de lumiere (vision scotopique)
    > Correct : les bâtonnets fonctionnent en faible luminosité, c’est leur avantage principal.
- [ ] Ils permettent la vision des couleurs
    > Incorrect : les bâtonnets ne perçoivent que les niveaux de gris.
- [x] Ils sont plus nombreux que les cones (environ 10 fois plus)
    > Correct : il y a environ 10^8 bâtonnets contre 10^7 cônes.
- [x] Apres adaptation a l'obscurite, un bâtonnet peut repondre a un seul photon
    > Correct : la sensibilité extrême des bâtonnets adaptés est l’une des propriétés les plus remarquables du système visuel.
- [ ] Ils sont concentres principalement dans la fovea
    > Incorrect : les bâtonnets sont situés en périphérie de la rétine ; la fovéa est dominée par les cônes.


### Quelle est la plage dynamique instantanée de l’œil humain ?

> Compare avec la plage dynamique après adaptation complète et avec celle des écrans actuels.

1. [ ] 3 f-stops
1. [ ] 14 f-stops
1. [x] 6,5 f-stops
    > Correct : la plage dynamique instantanée est d’environ 6,5 f-stops (environ 5 ordres de grandeur). La plage totale après adaptation est de 46,5 f-stops.
1. [ ] 46,5 f-stops
    > Incorrect : 46,5 f-stops correspond à la plage dynamique totale après adaptation complète à la lumière ou à l’obscurité.


### Où se situe la tache aveugle (blind spot) dans l’œil humain ?

> Pense à l’endroit où les fibres nerveuses quittent l’œil.

1. [ ] Au centre de la fovea
1. [ ] A la peripherie de la retine
1. [x] Au niveau du disque optique
    > Correct : le disque optique (optic disc) est le point de sortie du nerf optique. Il ne contient aucun photorécepteur, creant ainsi la tache aveugle.
1. [ ] Sur la cornee

text:
Level 2 — Comprehension

### Quelle est la principale difference fonctionnelle entre les cellules M et les cellules P ganglionnaires ?

> Pense au compromis entre resolution spatiale et resolution temporelle.

1. [ ] Les cellules M traitent les couleurs, les cellules P traitent le mouvement
1. [x] Les cellules M ont une meilleure resolution temporelle, les cellules P une meilleure resolution spatiale
    > Correct : les cellules M (magnocellulaires) ont une bonne resolution temporelle et sensibilite lumineuse mais pas de sensibilite chromatique. Les cellules P (parvocellulaires) ont une bonne resolution spatiale et sont sensibles aux couleurs.
1. [ ] Les cellules M et P ont les memes proprietes mais sont localisees differemment
1. [ ] Les cellules M sont plus petites et plus lentes que les cellules P
    > Incorrect : c'est l'inverse — les cellules M sont plus grandes et ont des vitesses de conduction plus rapides.


### Quelles affirmations decrivent correctement les proprietes des cellules simples (Simple Cells) de V1 ?

> Rappelle-toi les travaux de Hubel et Wiesel sur le cortex visuel primaire.

- [x] Elles repondent preferentiellement a des bords orientes dans une direction specifique
    > Correct : les cellules simples sont les detecteurs de bords orientes — leur propriete fondamentale.
- [x] Leur reponse peut etre construite a partir de plusieurs cellules centre-pourtour alignees
    > Correct : c'est le modele de construction des cellules simples a partir des RGC.
- [ ] Elles sont independantes de la position du stimulus dans le champ visuel
    > Incorrect : c'est une propriete des cellules complexes, pas des cellules simples.
- [ ] Elles sont situees dans le noyau geniculé latéral (LGN)
    > Incorrect : les cellules simples sont situees dans le cortex visuel primaire (V1), pas dans le LGN.
- [x] Elles constituent la premiere etape dans la hierarchie centre-pourtour vers complexe
    > Correct : la hierarchie est bien Centre-Pourtour, puis Simple, puis Complexe.


### Dans le flux ventral (Ventral Stream), que se passe-t-il a mesure qu'on s'eloigne de V1 vers les aires temporales superieures ?

> Pense aux deux tendances observees dans la progression le long du flux ventral.

1. [ ] Les champs recepteurs deviennent plus petits et la specificite diminue
1. [x] Les champs recepteurs s'agrandissent et la tolerance a la position augmente
    > Correct : dans le flux ventral, les champs recepteurs (RF) grandissent progressivement (de ~1 degre en V1 a ~12 degres dans TE) et les reponses deviennent de plus en plus independantes de la position exacte du stimulus (view independence).
1. [ ] Les champs recepteurs restent stables mais la sensibilite chromatique augmente
1. [ ] La latence de reponse diminue a mesure qu'on monte dans la hierarchie
    > Incorrect : la latence augmente de 40-60 ms en V1 a 80-100 ms dans TE.


### Pourquoi l'organisation centre-pourtour des cellules ganglionnaires est-elle avantageuse ?

> Pense a ce que les objets ont en commun : ils ne sont pas definis par leur luminosite absolue.

1. [ ] Elle permet de detecter les couleurs plus precisement
1. [ ] Elle augmente la sensibilite aux faibles niveaux de lumiere absolue
1. [x] Elle code les differences de luminosite plutot que les valeurs absolues, permettant l'amplification du signal sans saturation
    > Correct : les objets sont definis par leurs differences de luminosite avec l'arriere-plan. Coder les differences evite de devoir representer l'enormité de la gamme des valeurs absolues — c'est la base de la perception des objets.
1. [ ] Elle reduit la quantite d'information envoyee au cerveau par compression


### Quelle est la difference entre le flux dorsal et le flux ventral ?

> Pense aux questions auxquelles chaque flux repond.

1. [ ] Le flux dorsal traite les couleurs, le flux ventral traite le mouvement
1. [x] Le flux dorsal traite la localisation et le mouvement (ou ?), le flux ventral traite la reconnaissance (quoi ?)
    > Correct : le flux dorsal (Where stream) va vers le cortex parietal et gere la localisation spatiale et la perception du mouvement. Le flux ventral (What stream) va vers le cortex temporal inferieur et gere la reconnaissance des objets.
1. [ ] Les deux flux traitent les memes informations mais a des vitesses differentes
1. [ ] Le flux dorsal est responsable de la vision consciente, le flux ventral de la vision inconsciente


### Qu'est-ce que la presbytie et quelle en est la cause ?

> Pense au processus d'accommodation et a ce qui change avec l'age.

1. [ ] Une deformation de la cornee rendant l'image floue a toutes les distances
1. [ ] Une reduction du diametre de la pupille en fonction de l'age
1. [x] Une reduction de la plage d'accommodation due au durcissement progressif du cristallin
    > Correct : avec l'age, le cristallin durcit et les muscles ciliaires ne peuvent plus modifier sa forme suffisamment. La plage passe d'environ 8 cm - infini a 16 ans a environ 50 cm - infini a 50 ans.
1. [ ] Une diminution du nombre de cones dans la fovea


### Le conflit vergence-accommodation (Vergence-Accommodation Conflict) dans les affichages stereoscopiques provient de :

> Pense a ce que font les yeux dans le monde reel par rapport a ce qui se passe devant un ecran 3D classique.

1. [ ] Une frequence de rafraichissement trop basse de l'ecran
1. [ ] Une disparite binoculaire excessive entre les deux images
1. [x] Un decouplage entre la distance de convergence des yeux et la distance de mise au point sur l'ecran physique
    > Correct : dans le monde reel, vergence et accommodation sont couplee a la meme distance. Sur un ecran stereo, les yeux convergent vers la position 3D percue mais doivent accommoder sur l'ecran physique (distance fixe) — c'est le conflit.
1. [ ] Une difference de luminance entre les images gauche et droite

title: The Human Visual System — Quiz
text:
Level 3 — Mastery

### Remets les etapes de l'evolution de l'oeil dans le bon ordre chronologique.

> Pense a la sequence evolutive depuis les organismes les plus simples jusqu'a l'oeil des vertebres.

1. Tache de cellules photosensibles sans direction
2. Zone deprimee permettant une sensibilite directionnelle limitee
3. Oeil stenope avec chambre remplie d'eau
4. Developpement d'un cristallin distinct
5. Iris et cornee separes formant l'oeil vertebre complet


### Remets les etapes de la voie visuelle dans l'ordre, depuis l'oeil jusqu'au cortex.

> Pense au chemin emprunte par l'information visuelle depuis la retine jusqu'au traitement cortical.

1. Retine (photorécepteurs et cellules ganglionnaires)
2. Nerf optique (Optic Nerve)
3. Chiasma optique (Optic Chiasm)
4. Noyau Geniculé Lateral (LGN)
5. Cortex visuel primaire (V1)


### Un patient presente une lesion isolee du flux ventral (Ventral Stream). Quel deficit est le plus probable ?

> Pense aux fonctions specifiques du flux ventral par opposition au flux dorsal.

1. [ ] Incapacite a localiser les objets dans l'espace
    > Incorrect : la localisation spatiale est une fonction du flux dorsal (Where stream).
1. [ ] Perte de la vision peripherique
    > Incorrect : la vision peripherique n'est pas specifiquement associee au flux ventral.
1. [x] Incapacite a reconnaitre les objets (agnosie visuelle) malgre une capacite de localisation preservee
    > Correct : des lesions du flux ventral produisent des deficits de reconnaissance (agnosie visuelle, prosopagnosie) tout en preservant la capacite a localiser et eviter les obstacles.
1. [ ] Perte de la perception du mouvement
    > Incorrect : la perception du mouvement est une fonction du flux dorsal et de l'aire MT.


### Un ingenieur conçoit un affichage VR et souhaite eliminer le conflit vergence-accommodation. Quelles technologies permettent reellement de le resoudre ?

> Pense aux technologies qui reproduisent le comportement optique du monde reel plutot que de simuler une image 2D sur un ecran plat.

- [ ] Augmenter la frequence de rafraichissement a 120 Hz
    > Incorrect : la frequence de rafraichissement ne resout pas le conflit vergence-accommodation — les deux restent decouples.
- [x] Affichages a champ de lumiere (Light Field Displays)
    > Correct : les affichages a champ de lumiere reproduisent les rayons lumineux provenant de differentes profondeurs, permettant une accommodation naturelle.
- [x] Affichages holographiques (Holographic Displays)
    > Correct : les affichages holographiques reproduisent le front d'onde complet de la lumiere — solution ultime pour eliminer le conflit.
- [ ] Augmenter la resolution de l'ecran
    > Incorrect : une resolution plus elevee ameliore la nettete mais ne resout pas le decouplage vergence-accommodation.
- [x] Affichages a focus contingent du regard (Gaze-Contingent Focus Displays)
    > Correct : en combinant eye-tracking et optique variable, ces affichages ajustent dynamiquement la zone de nettete selon ou regarde l'utilisateur.


### La fonction de sensibilite au contraste (Contrast Sensitivity Function, CSF) du systeme visuel humain presente un pic de sensibilite a environ :

> Pense a l'unite de mesure utilisee pour la frequence spatiale et aux valeurs associees aux limites du systeme visuel.

1. [ ] 1 cycle par degre (cpd)
1. [x] 4 a 6 cycles par degre (cpd)
    > Correct : la CSF atteint son pic de sensibilite entre 4 et 6 cpd. En dessous, la sensibilite diminue (inhibition laterale) ; au-dessus aussi (limite de resolution liee a la densite des cones, environ 60 cpd).
1. [ ] 60 cycles par degre (cpd)
    > Incorrect : 60 cpd correspond a la limite superieure de resolution liee a la densite des cones dans la fovea, pas au pic de sensibilite.
1. [ ] 120 cycles par degre (cpd)


### Quelles affirmations sur le Noyau Geniculé Lateral (LGN) sont correctes ?

> Rappelle-toi la structure en couches du LGN et ses connexions avec les cellules ganglionnaires.

- [x] Le LGN contient deux couches magnocellulaires alimentees par les cellules M
    > Correct : les deux couches magnocellulaires recoivent les signaux des cellules M a meilleure resolution temporelle.
- [x] Le LGN contient quatre couches parvocellulaires alimentees par les cellules P
    > Correct : les quatre couches parvocellulaires recoivent les signaux des cellules P a meilleure resolution spatiale et sensibilite chromatique.
- [ ] Il y a un seul LGN partage entre les deux hemispheres
    > Incorrect : il y a un LGN dans chaque hemisphere cerebral.
- [x] Toutes les couches du LGN maintiennent l'organisation retinotopique
    > Correct : la retinotopie (correspondance spatiale entre retine et cortex) est preservee dans toutes les couches du LGN.
- [ ] Le LGN est un simple relais passif sans traitement propre
    > Incorrect : le LGN integre des signaux de retour (feedback) depuis V1 et d'autres structures — c'est un noeud actif de controle.


### Quelle innovation du neocognitron de Fukushima a ete directement reprise dans les reseaux de neurones convolutionnels (CNN) modernes ?

> Pense au principe architectural fondamental qui permet l'invariance a la translation.

1. [ ] L'utilisation de la retropropagation du gradient pour l'apprentissage
    > Incorrect : le neocognitron utilisait un apprentissage non supervise, pas la retropropagation. C'est LeCun qui a introduit la retropropagation dans les CNN.
1. [x] L'alternance de couches de detection de caracteristiques (simples) et de couches de regroupement spatial (complexes)
    > Correct : l'alternance couches S (simples, equivalentes a la convolution) et couches C (complexes, equivalentes au pooling) est le principe fondateur repris dans les CNN.
1. [ ] L'utilisation de donnees d'entrainement labelisees en grande quantite
1. [ ] La connexion totale entre toutes les couches du reseau
    > Incorrect : le neocognitron utilisait des connexions locales et partagees — principe oppose aux couches entierement connectees.


### Un utilisateur ressent des nausees et de la fatigue oculaire apres 30 minutes d'utilisation d'un casque VR. Quelle en est la cause la plus probable du point de vue du systeme visuel ?

> Pense au phenomene specifique aux affichages stereoscopiques classiques qui cree une incoherence dans le systeme visuel.

1. [ ] La resolution trop elevee de l'affichage fatigue les photorécepteurs
1. [ ] La frequence de rafraichissement trop basse provoque un scintillement perceptible
1. [x] Le conflit vergence-accommodation cree une incoherence entre les signaux oculomoteurs et visuels
    > Correct : le conflit vergence-accommodation est la cause principale de l'inconfort, de la fatigue visuelle et des nausees lors de l'utilisation prolongee de casques VR stereoscopiques classiques.
1. [ ] La luminosite excessive de l'ecran sature les cones


### Quelle est la relation correcte entre les cellules simples de V1 et les cellules centre-pourtour du LGN ?

> Pense a la construction hierarchique des reponses neuronales.

1. [ ] Les cellules simples de V1 sont des copies identiques des cellules centre-pourtour
1. [ ] Les cellules centre-pourtour se transforment directement en cellules complexes sans passer par les cellules simples
1. [x] Une cellule simple peut etre construite a partir de plusieurs cellules centre-pourtour alignees selon un axe preferentiel
    > Correct : l'alignement spatial de plusieurs cellules centre-pourtour crée la selectivite a l'orientation des cellules simples — c'est le modele de Hubel et Wiesel.
1. [ ] Les cellules simples de V1 recoivent directement les signaux des photorécepteurs sans passer par le LGN


### Parmi les caracteristiques suivantes, lesquelles constituent de reelles limitations de l'oeil humain ?

> Il s'agit ici de distinguer les proprietes normales des vraies imperfections du systeme visuel.

- [x] L'image formee sur la retine est inversee
    > Correct : la lumiere traversant le cristallin forme une image renversee sur la retine. Le cerveau corrige cette inversion.
- [x] La haute resolution est limitee a la zone foveale
    > Correct : la vision haute resolution n'existe que dans la fovea, qui couvre environ 2 degres du champ visuel.
- [ ] L'oeil ne peut voir que trois couleurs primaires
    > Incorrect : ce n'est pas une limitation — c'est le principe meme du systeme trichromate qui permet de percevoir toutes les couleurs visibles.
- [x] Les vaisseaux sanguins se trouvent devant les photorécepteurs
    > Correct : l'organisation inversee de la retine humaine place les vaisseaux et les neurones devant les photorécepteurs, ce qui est une imperfection anatomique.
- [x] La tache aveugle au niveau du disque optique
    > Correct : l'absence de photorécepteurs au point de sortie du nerf optique cree une zone sans vision que le cerveau comble par interpolation.


### Quelle etait la contribution specifique de Kepler a la comprehension de la vision, au-dela de ce qu'Alhazen avait etabli ?

> Pense au probleme specifique qu'Alhazen n'avait pas resolu correctement.

1. [ ] Demonstrer que la lumiere voyage en lignes droites
    > Incorrect : c'est une contribution d'Alhazen.
1. [ ] Proposer que les objets envoient de la lumiere vers l'oeil
    > Incorrect : c'est la contribution fondamentale d'Alhazen, pas de Kepler.
1. [x] Expliquer comment le cristallin separe les rayons provenant de differents points de la scene pour former une image nette sur la retine
    > Correct : Kepler a compris que les rayons provenant de directions differentes, meme s'ils arrivent au meme point du cristallin, sont refractes dans des directions differentes et separés, formant une image nette. Alhazen pensait a tort que seul le rayon perpendiculaire contribuait a la vision.
1. [ ] Decourir l'existence des batonnets et des cones dans la retine
    > Incorrect : la decouverte des photorécepteurs est bien posterieure a Kepler.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Vision is one of the most sophisticated senses developed by the animal kingdom. Understanding how living things perceive the visual world is fundamental to designing artificial imaging systems, computer vision algorithms, and advanced display devices.
The human visual system (Human Visual System, HVS) is the result of millions of years of evolution. To fully understand it, it is useful to place it in its biological and historical context.



Life on Earth has evolved over hundreds of millions of years, gradually developing increasingly efficient visual systems.
The geological timeline allows us to locate the appearance of different species and, by extension, the emergence of their ocular systems:

Paleozoic Era: appearance of the first marine species with rudimentary photosensitive structures
Mesozoic Era: development of reptiles, birds and first mammals
Cenozoic Era: emergence of higher mammals and finally hominids







TipIntuition



The eye did not appear suddenly. It is an organ that evolved in stages, from simple photosensitive cells to the complex structures seen today in vertebrates.







The oldest biological visual systems are found in marine creatures:

Nautilus belauensis (~450 million years): has a pinhole eye type, without a lens. The image is formed by a very small hole which limits the incoming light. The resolution is low but the mechanism is extremely robust.
Octopus / Octopus (~200 million years): developed a very efficient lens eye, capable of detecting contrasts and movements with great precision. Remarkably, the octopus is colorblind despite its sophisticated eye.





Reptiles (~200 million years): lens eye with a pupil often in a vertical slit, allowing fine control of incoming light.
Spiders (~130 million years old): evolved multiple eyes with different functions — some for peripheral vision, others for high-resolution frontal vision.
Birds (~155 million years): have visual acuity often greater than that of humans (raptors), sometimes with two distinct foveas.
Mammals (~125 million years): developed stereoscopic vision, essential for depth perception.




The human lineage dates back about 3 million years (Australopithecus afarensis → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo neanderthalensis → Homo sapiens).
The human visual system is strongly biased toward binocular frontal vision, allowing for excellent depth perception — a key adaptation for tree-dwelling primates.




The modern eye did not appear spontaneously. Biologists have reconstructed a plausible evolutionary sequence in several stages:







Step
Description




(a) Photosensitive cell region
Simple spot of cells reacting to light, directionless


(b) Depressed/folded area
Allows limited directional sensitivity


(c) Pinhole eye
Formation of a blurry but directional image


(d) Chamber with transparent fluid
Improves light transmission


(e) Development of a distinct lens
Allows image focusing


(f) Iris and cornea separated
Complete structure of the vertebrate eye









NoteTo remember



The human eye as we know it—with cornea, lens, retina, iris, and humors—is the result of a long chain of gradual evolutions, each providing a selective advantage.
