title: The Human Visual System
text:
Extromissive theories
Before modern understanding of light and optics, ancient thinkers proposed very different theories of vision.

Plato and the theory of visual fire (350 BC)
Plato proposed an extromissive theory: the eyes emit light similar to that of the sun, which mixes with external light to produce vision.
This tripartite vision required:

Innate light emanating from the eyes (main cause)
The exterior light related to our interior light
Light coming from visible objects themselves







WarningWarning



These theories, although false, have dominated thinking for centuries. They illustrate how correct observations (we see things) can lead to incorrect explanations.




Difficulties of extromissive theories
These theories have encountered many logical objections:

Why do we instantly see very distant objects as soon as we open our eyes?
Why don’t the visual systems of different people looking at the same object interfere?
What happens if the eyes are closed when the visual mind returns?
Aristotle (330 BC) proposed that objects create “material images” carried by the atmosphere, but how do large images fit into such a small eye?

title: The Human Visual System
section: Alhazen and the modern theory of vision (1040)
text:
Alhazen and the modern theory of vision (1040)
Abu Ali al-Hassan ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen, is considered the greatest optical scientist of the Middle Ages.
His major contributions:

Self-luminous bodies emit light (sun, moon, flame)
Light travels in straight lines
When light hits an object, it radiates in all directions
Distinction between transparent and opaque media
Pointillist theory of vision: we see a collection of points on the surfaces of objects
Geometric theory explaining the one-to-one correspondence between the world and the image formed in our eyes







TipIntuition



Alhazen reverses the paradigm: it is no longer the eye which emits light towards objects, but the objects which send light towards the eye. This conceptual reversal is fundamental.



Alhazen’s problem and refraction
Alhazen encountered an important problem: since light from one point on a surface reaches the entire surface of the eye, how can we only see a single image?
His answer (incorrect but ingenious): only the ray entering perpendicular to the eye contributes to vision; the other rays are more refracted and therefore “weakened”.
In reality, the optical properties of the lens combine all these rays into a single focal point — this is the principle of focusing.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Image formation
The formation of an image obeys the laws of geometric optics:

A ray of light leaves the source and travels in a straight line
When hitting an object, it is reflected (reflection) and/or refracted (refraction)
If the object is a crystalline lens, the light useful for imaging is refracted light.

Refraction is described by the Snell-Descartes law, which establishes the link between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction based on the refractive indices of the two media.

title: The Human Visual System
section: Johannes Kepler and the retinal theory (1571–1630)
text:
Johannes Kepler and the retinal theory (1571–1630)
Kepler is the founder of modern theories of optics and light. Its fundamental principles:

Light is emitted by its source and travels to distant locations
From any point, light travels in an infinite number of straight lines
Light can travel to infinity
These emission lines are straight and are called rays


Kepler’s retinal theory
Kepler brilliantly solved Alhazen’s problem:
Although light rays from many points on a surface reach the same point on the lens, they arrive there from different directions. They are therefore refracted in different directions and separated by the lens, thus forming a clear image on the retina.






NoteTo remember



Kepler established that it is the retina — and not the pupil or the lens — which is the seat of the image formed by the eye. This is the basis of all modern physiological optics.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Modern theories of vision
Three major trends contribute to our current understanding:

Psychology of perception: identifies the functionalities of the visual system (what can we see? with what precision?)
Neurophysiology: provides mechanistic explanations (how do neurons process visual information?)
Computational Vision: poses new problems in seeking to reproduce vision in machines


Modern Understanding of Human Vision
Human vision is generally divided into two levels:

Low-level vision (Low-level / Early Vision): parallel processing, multiplexing, partitioning. Concerns the detection of simple primitives (edges, colors, movements).
High-level Vision: modularity, object recognition, scene interpretation.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Overview of HVS
The human visual system is a visual information processing pipeline that begins at the eyes (sensors) and ends in the visual cortex (high-level processing).





flowchart LR
    A[Yeux\nCapteurs] --> B[Nerf optique\nRéseau]
    B --> C[Cortex visuel\nCalcul]
    A --> D[Traitement bas niveau]
    C --> E[Traitement haut niveau]

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Visual Acuity
Visual acuity is the ability to distinguish fine details.

The notation 20/20 is the reference for normal vision: it corresponds to approximately 1 minute of arc of angular resolution.
An acuity of 20/200 means that the patient sees at 20 feet what a normal person sees at 200 feet.







TipIntuition



1 minute of arc corresponds to approximately 0.017° — it is the ability to distinguish two points separated by approximately 1.5 mm at a distance of 5 meters.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Field of View
The human visual field is remarkably wide:

Horizontal: approximately 200° in total

~120° in binocular vision (binocular)
~40° in monocular vision on each side

Vertical: approximately 135°

The central viewing area (60°) offers the best resolution. Upper peripheral vision extends to 30°, and lower peripheral vision to 40–45°.






NoteTo remember



Binocular vision — that is, the area where both eyes see simultaneously — is essential for depth perception (stereopia). It covers approximately 120° in the center of the visual field.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Temporal Resolution

The human visual system has a temporal resolution of approximately 60 Hz (depends on contrast and luminance).
Below this frequency, we perceive flickering. Above, the movement appears continuous.

This is why modern displays aim for 60Hz or higher for a smooth display.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Dynamic Range
Dynamic range measures the ratio of maximum to minimum brightness a system can perceive.

Instantaneous range: 6.5 f-stops (~5 orders of magnitude)
Adapted range (after dark or light adaptation): up to 46.5 f-stops (~14 orders of magnitude)




System
Dynamic Range




Instant human vision
~5 orders of magnitude


Adapted human vision
~14 orders of magnitude


Current views
~3 orders of magnitude









TipIntuition



The human eye is far superior to current displays in terms of dynamic range. This is why HDR (High Dynamic Range) techniques seek to reproduce this tonal richness.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Color

Color vision covers the entire CIE xy diagram
Perceptual distances are linear in CIE Lab space — that is, two equidistant colors in CIE Lab appear equally different to the human eye

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Accommodation Range
Accommodation is the ability of the eye to focus at different distances:

At 16 years: from ~8 cm to infinity
At 50 years: from ~50 cm to infinity (the range reduces considerably with age)

This phenomenon is due to the progressive hardening of the lens, leading to presbyopia.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
General structure
The human eye is a spherical organ approximately 24 mm in diameter. Its main structures:

Cornea (Cornea): rounded transparent surface in front of the eye. Ensures approximately 70% of the total refraction of the eye.
Iris: pigmented diaphragm which regulates the diameter of the pupil.
Pupil: central orifice of the iris through which light passes.
Crystalline (Lens): biconvex lens whose curvature is modified by the ciliary muscles for accommodation.
Anterior Chamber: filled with aqueous humor.
Posterior Chamber: between the iris and the lens.
Vitreous Body (Vitreous Humor): transparent gel filling the posterior part of the eye.
Retina (Retina): layer of photosensitive cells lining the back of the eye.
Choroid (Choroid): vascular nourishing layer between the retina and the sclera.
Sclera (Sclera): white, tough outer layer of the eye.
Fovea: central area of ​​the retina with the highest density of cones — seat of high-resolution vision.
Optic Disc: exit point of the optic nerve, absence of photoreceptors → blind spot.
Optic Nerve: transmits visual signals to the brain.







TipIntuition



We can compare the eye to a camera: the cornea and the crystalline lens are the lenses, the iris is the diaphragm, and the retina is the photographic sensor. But this analogy has important limits which we will see later.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Three-layer structure
The retina is organized into three main layers of cells:

Outer layer — Receptor cells: cones and rods, the primary photoreceptors
Middle layer — Collector cells: bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells
Inner layer — Retinal ganglion cells (Retinal Ganglion Cells, RGC): whose axons form the optic nerve







NoteTo remember



Paradoxically, light passes through the layers of ganglion and bipolar cells before reaching the photoreceptors, which are located at the back of the retina. This is a so-called “inverse” organization compared to a camera.

title: The Human Visual System
section: The fundamental trade-off: sensitivity vs. resolution
text:
The fundamental trade-off: sensitivity vs. resolution
The retina makes a fundamental trade-off between:

Light sensitivity (via rods)
Spatial resolution (via cones)

This compromise is managed by two parallel systems.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
The two parallel systems

Scotopic system — Rods

Number: ~10⁸ rods in the human retina
Sensitivity: very high — sensitive to low light levels (scotopic vision)
Convergence: strong convergence towards the collecting and ganglion cells
Result: low resolution image but persists even in low light
Color: none — grayscale vision only







TipIntuition



The convergence of the rods is like adding the signals of many pixels to make one — we gain in sensitivity (signal) but we lose in resolution (detail).




Photopic system — Cones

Number: ~10⁷ cones in the human retina
Sensitivity: high light levels (photopic vision)
Convergence: very limited — some foveal cones have an almost 1-to-1 connection
Result: high resolution image in good brightness
Color: yes — color vision

title: The Human Visual System
text:
The three types of cones
Cones are divided into three types according to their spectral sensitivity:



Type
Sensitivity
Maximum wavelength




S (Shorts)
Blue
~419nm


M (Medium)
Green
~531nm


L (Long)
Red
~559nm









WarningImportant



The bandwidth of the optic nerve is insufficient to transmit all the raw signals from the photoreceptors. This involves coding of visual information from the retina — this is the beginning of visual processing.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Photoreceptor mosaic
Rods and cones can be seen as eye’s pixels.

Distribution on the retina

Blind spot (Blind spot / Optic disc): no photoreceptor
Fovea: maximum density of cones (~180 × 10³/mm²), few rods
Periphery: dominated by rods, with a maximum density between 15° and 20° eccentricity

This organization explains why:

Daylight vision is best in the center of the visual field
Night vision is best slightly off center (look slightly sideways to see a faint star)

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Extreme sensitivity of the sticks
After dark adaptation, a single rod can respond to a single photon.
This extraordinary sensitivity is due to the phototransduction cascade: a single photon activates a rhodopsin molecule, which triggers an enzymatic cascade amplifying the signal by a factor ~10⁶.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Spectral response of photoreceptors
The spectral response of the cones has important characteristics:

S cones (blue): weak response, peak at ~419 nm
M cones (green): dominant response, peak at ~531 nm
L cones (red): response extending towards infrared, peak at ~559 nm
Sticks: peak at ~496 nm (between blue and green)







TipIntuition



The fact that M (green) cones dominate explains why our sensitivity is maximal in green under photopic conditions. This is also why safety signs are often green or yellow-green.

title: The Human Visual System
section: Limitations of the human visual system
text:
Limitations of the human visual system
Despite its remarkable performance, the human eye has several notable limitations:

Blood vessels and other cells located in front of the photoreceptors (partially obscure the view)
Shadows cast on photoreceptors → non-uniform brightness
The image on the retina is inverted! (the brain corrects it)
High resolution only in the fovea (a single fovea in humans, compared to several in some birds and cheetahs)
The blind spot at the optic disc

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Role and function
Retinal Ganglion Cells (RGCs) constitute the first stage of visual processing.
Their main function: to replace absolute brightness levels with a retinotopic map of differences.






TipIntuition



Objects are not associated with a particular absolute brightness, but with differences in brightness between them and their background. This is why a white object looks white both in direct sunlight and indoors — it’s always lighter than what’s around it.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Center-Surround organization
The ganglion cells have a receptive field (receptive field) organized in an antagonistic center and perimeter:

On-center (off-surround) cells: activate when light illuminates the center and not the perimeter
Off-center (on-surround) cells: activate when the perimeter is illuminated but not the center

This organization makes it possible to amplify the differences in brightness without having to represent the enormous range of absolute values. It is the basis of the perception of objects.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Partition M and P
Ganglion cells are divided into two main classes:

M Cells (Magnocellular)

Receive signals from a large number of photoreceptors
Advantage: good sensitivity to light, excellent temporal resolution
Disadvantage: low spatial resolution
Are taller, have faster nerve conduction velocities
More transient responses (adapt quickly)
No color sensitivity
Main role: perception of movement, detection of sudden stimuli



P cells (Parvocellular)

Receive signals from a small number of photoreceptors
Advantage: excellent spatial resolution
Disadvantage: low temporal resolution
Color sensitivity (chromatic)
Main role: color, texture, patterns — major role in object recognition







NoteTo remember



The M system manages the when and the where (temporal, movement), while the P system manages the what (spatial, color, details). This division of labor is a fundamental architectural principle of the visual system.


These two types of cells respectively supply the magnocellular (2 layers) and parvocellular (4 layers) layers of the Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN).

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Accommodation
Accommodation is the ability of the eye to adapt its focal length to see clearly at different distances.
Mechanism:

Far vision: the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the zonular fibers are tense, the lens is flattened (less convergent)
Close vision: the ciliary muscles contract, the zonular fibers relax, the lens bulges (more convergent)

The range of accommodation decreases with age (presbyopia):

16 years old: ~8 cm to infinity
50 years: ~50 cm to infinity

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Oculomotor processes and visual cues
Depth perception uses two types of complementary mechanisms:

Stereopsy (Binocular)

Oculomotor cue: Vergence — both eyes converge towards the same point thanks to the extraocular muscles
Visual cue: Binocular disparity — the two eyes see slightly different images that the brain merges into 3D perception



Monocular cues

Oculomotor cue: Accommodation — tension of the ciliary muscles informs the focusing distance
Visual Cue: Retinal Blur — out-of-focus objects are blurred, indicating relative distances

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Refractive Errors
When image formation does not occur correctly on the retina:








Condition
Description
Correction




Emmétropia (Emmetropia)

None


Myopia (Myopia)
Close view — focus in front of the retina
Concave (divergent) lens


Hypermetropia (Hypermetropia)
Far view — focus behind the retina
Convex (convergent) lens


Astigmatism (Astigmatism)
Irregular curvature — no single focus
Cylindrical lens

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Visual Pathways
After the retina, the visual signal takes several routes:

Optic nerve (Optic Nerve): bundle of axons of retinal ganglion cells
Optic Chiasm (Optic Chiasm): the nasal fibers (temporal field) cross towards the opposite hemisphere
Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (Lateral Geniculate Nucleus, LGN): main thalamic relay
Superior Colliculus: control of eye movements
Primary Visual Cortex (Primary Visual Cortex, V1): first cortical processing







NoteTo remember



The left visual field is processed by the right hemisphere, and vice versa. This partial decussation at the optic chiasm allows a cross-representation of the visual field.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
The Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
The LGN is the main relay between the retina and the visual cortex:

One LGN in each cerebral hemisphere
2 magnocellular layers: powered by M cells — better temporal resolution
4 parvocellular layers: powered by P cells — better spatial resolution and spectral sensitivity

All layers maintain the retinotopy organization: neighboring neurons in the LGN process neighboring areas of the visual field.






TipIntuition



The LGN is not a simple passive relay — it integrates feedback signals from the visual cortex and other structures. It is an active control node for visual processing.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
The Primary Visual Cortex (V1)
David H. Hubel and Torsten N. Wiesel received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1981 for their pioneering work on the primary visual cortex (1962).

The three cell types of V1

1. Center-Surround Cells
Similar to ganglion cells — respond to points of light in an antagonistic center-perimeter context.


2. Simple Cells

Similar to core-perimeter cells but with elongated excitatory and inhibitory regions
Respond to oriented edges at a specific position and orientation in the visual field
Selective to orientation of the stimulus (bar of light, edge)







TipIntuition



A simple cell can be thought of as an oriented edge detector: it responds strongly when a bar of light is in the right orientation (e.g., vertical at 45°) and at the right position, but not at other orientations.


The response of a single cell can be constructed from multiple center-perimeter cells aligned along a preferential axis.


3. Complex Cells

Process a more abstract type of visual information
Partially independent of the exact location in the visual field
Selective to orientation but tolerant to the exact position of the stimulus




Sensitivity to the orientation of V1
The classic experiment of Hubel and Wiesel shows that V1 cells respond strongly to bars oriented in a preferential direction, weakly to close orientations, and almost not to orthogonal orientations.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Hypercolumns
The spatial organization of V1 minimizes the distance between neurons processing similar stimuli along three dimensions:

Original eye (left or right)
Preferred orientation
Retinotopic localization

This organization is the striate module model, sometimes illustrated by the model of orientation columns in monkeys.






NoteTakeaways — Hebb’s Rule



Hebb’s rule: “neurons that fire together wire together”. This Hebbian learning rule explains how the functional organization of V1 emerges from visual experience.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
The Contrast Sensitivity Function (CSF)
The CSF describes the sensitivity of the visual system to contrast as a function of spatial frequency:

Peak sensitivity at 4–6 cycles per degree (cpd)
Decay at high frequencies (resolution limit ~60 cpd, linked to cone density)
Decay at low frequencies (due to lateral inhibition)
The CSF moves according to viewing distance







TipIntuition



The CSF explains why compressed JPEG images, which remove high frequencies, still appear acceptable — the visual system is less sensitive to very high spatial frequencies.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Visual processing areas
Beyond V1, visual processing is organized into a hierarchy of specialized areas (V2, V3, V3A, V4, V5/MT, etc.), each processing increasingly abstract aspects of visual information.
The neurons show increasing specificity as we move up the hierarchy:

V1: simple oriented edges
V2: edge combinations
V4: color, complex shapes
IT (Inferior Temporal): objects, faces

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Dorsal and Ventral Streams
The visual cortex is organized into two main pathways after V1:

Ventral Flow — The What

Path: V1 → V2 → V4 → TEO → TE (inferior temporal cortex)
Specialized in object recognition: color, texture, shape, identity
Receptive fields gradually enlarge
View independence increases

Dorsal Flow — The Where (Where)

Path: V1 → V2 → V3 → MT/MST → Parietal cortex

Answers the questions “where is the object?” » and “how does it move?” »







NoteTo remember



The dissociation between dorsal and ventral streams is illustrated by neurological cases: patients with lesions of the ventral stream can locate objects but not identify them (visual agnosia); the reverse is also possible.

title: The Human Visual System
section: Fusiform Face Area (FFA) and Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA)
text:
Fusiform Face Area (FFA) and Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA)
Two specialized regions deserve mention:

FFA (Fusiform Face Area): activates selectively for human faces. Also enabled for categories of intense visual expertise (e.g. cars among automotive experts).
PPA (Parahippocampal Place Area): activates for places and scenes (interiors, landscapes).

title: The Human Visual System
section: Intrinsic and extrinsic connectivity of the ventral flow
text:
Intrinsic and extrinsic connectivity of the ventral flow
The ventral flow is not a simple feedforward chain. It includes:

Bidirectional connections between adjacent areas
Feedback connections from upper areas to V1
Connections with the amygdala (emotional processing) and the prefrontal cortex (attention, working memory)







WarningImportant



We now know that the ventral flow is much more complex than a simple sequence of feedforward steps. Bidirectional connections and feedback play an important role that has not yet been fully exploited in computer vision.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Neuroscience and computer vision synthesis
Several key principles:

Neurons show increasing specificity in the visual pathway
Simple and complex cells in V1 are orientation selective
Convolution with a linear kernel followed by simple nonlinearities is a good model for the retina, LGN and V1
Beyond V1, we do not yet have satisfactory computational models
Good visual systems architectures are probably hierarchical and “mostly” feedforward

title: The Human Visual System
text:
The Neocognitron (Neocognitron)
The neocognitron, proposed by Kunihiko Fukushima (NHK Broadcasting Science Research Laboratories), is a self-organized artificial neural network inspired by the hierarchy of Hubel and Wiesel:

Input → retina → LGN → simple cells → complex cells → hypercomplex cells → … → “grandmother” cell
Architecture: alternation of layers S (simple, feature detectors) and C (complex, pooling)
First architecture capable of translation-invariant pattern recognition







TipIntuition



The neocognitron is the direct precursor of convolutional neural networks (CNN). The central idea is the same: local filters followed by pooling to obtain position invariance.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets)
Yann LeCun, Léon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio and Patrick Haffner developed LeNet, applied to character recognition (MNIST) — founding article “Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition” (1998).
LeNet architecture:





flowchart LR
    A[Image\n28×28] --> B[Convolution\nC1 6@28×28]
    B --> C[Pooling\nS2 6@14×14]
    C --> D[Convolution\nC3 16@10×10]
    D --> E[Pooling\nS4 16@5×5]
    E --> F[Dense\nF5 120]
    F --> G[Dense\nF6 84]
    G --> H[Sortie\n10 classes]






Computer vision benefited from two major inspirations from HVS:

The orientation selectivity of simple and complex cells in V1 inspired descriptors like SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) and HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients)
The feedforward view of the ventral stream — with its alternating layers of simple and complex cells — led to the neocognitron and then to the convolutional networks that dominate modern computer vision

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Stereoscopic Displays

History
Stereoscopy exploits binocular disparity to create an illusion of depth:

Charles Wheatstone (1838) invents the stereoscope — the first display device using binocular vision
Stereoscopes used pairs of photos taken from two slightly offset positions (simulating both eyes)
176 years later: 3D glasses for cinema and television use exactly the same principle



Principle
By presenting each eye with a slightly different (horizontally offset) image, the brain merges the two into a coherent three-dimensional perception.

title: The Human Visual System
text:
Virtual Reality

Historical development



Epoch
Technology
Actors




1838
Stereoscopes
Wheatstone, Brewster


1968
Pioneering VR/AR
Ivan Sutherland (“Sword of Damocles”)


2012–present
VR explosion
Meta, Apple, Sony, …





Next generation technologies
Three main approaches for advanced VR/AR displays:

Gaze-Contingent Focus Displays: combine eye-tracking and variable optics to dynamically adjust the area of ​​focus depending on the direction of gaze
Near-eye Light Field Displays: reproduce the entire field of light, allowing natural accommodation
Holographic Displays: use holograms to reproduce the wavefront of light — ultimate but technically very demanding solution

title: The Human Visual System
text:
The Vergence-Accommodation Conflict

Description of the problem
In the real world, vergence and accommodation are coupled: the eyes converge and focus at the same distance.
In current stereoscopic displays, the eyes converge on the perceived position of the object (simulated 3D distance), but must accommodate on the physical screen (fixed distance). These two distances are different — this is the vergence-accommodation conflict.






WarningImportant



This conflict is fundamental and cannot be resolved by conventional stereoscopic displays. It requires radically different optical approaches (field of light, holography).




Adverse effects
The vergence-accommodation conflict can cause:

Visual discomfort
Visual fatigue
Nausea
Double vision (diplopic vision)
Eyestrain
Degradation of perceived image quality
Pathologies in the developing visual system (in children)



Comfort Zone (Zone of Comfort)
The comfort zone defines the binocular disparity range within which a user can comfortably view a stereoscopic display.
This area strongly depends on the viewing distance:

Cinema: large comfort zone (long distance)
Television: intermediate zone
Desktop: more restricted area
Mobile: very restricted area (very close)







TipIntuition



The closer one is to the screen, the more rapidly the vergence varies with distance — and therefore the more severe the vergence-accommodation conflict is for the same screen disparity.

title: Computational Imaging — Quiz
text:
### How many dimensions does the complete plenoptic function have?

> Consider the parameters needed to describe a light ray at any point in space.

1. [ ] 3
1. [ ] 4
1. [x] 5
    > Correct: The plenoptic function L(x, y, z, \theta, \phi) is defined on 5D space — 3 for spatial position and 2 for direction.
1. [ ] 7


### What is the main difference between conventional and computational photography?

> Consider the respective roles of optics and digital processing in each paradigm.

1. [ ] Computational photography uses a larger sensor.
1. [ ] Computational photography does not require a lens.
1. [x] In computational photography, optics and computation are co-designed: the captured image is a coded representation, not necessarily visually readable.
    > Correct: this is the founding principle. Generalized optics encode, generalized computation decodes. The raw image may be visually unreadable.
1. [ ] Computational photography only improves resolution.


### What properties characterize the pinhole camera?

> Compare the advantages and disadvantages against a lens camera.

- [x] Infinite depth of field — everything is in focus
    > Correct: an infinitesimally small aperture allows only one ray per source point, so everything is in focus.
- [ ] Very efficient with light
    > Incorrect: the infinitesimally small aperture transmits very few photons — this is one of its major flaws.
- [x] Very inefficient with light
    > Correct: small aperture = few photons collected.
- [ ] Only one plane is in focus
    > Incorrect: this is the characteristic of a lens camera, not a pinhole camera.


### Que représente la magnification m dans le système optique d'une caméra à lentille ?

> Pense à comment la taille de l'image change quand on modifie la distance lentille-capteur.

1. [ ] Le rapport entre la focale et la distance objet.
1. [x] Le rapport entre la focale f et la quantité (D' - f), où D' est la distance lentille-capteur.
    > Correct : m = f / (D' - f). Ce paramètre est crucial pour l'alignement des images d'une pile focale, car il change avec la mise au point.
1. [ ] La résolution du capteur divisée par la focale.
1. [ ] Le diamètre de l'ouverture divisé par la focale.


### What component is placed between the main lens and the sensor in a plenoptic camera?

> Consider what allows capturing angular information in addition to spatial information.

1. [ ] A low-pass filter
1. [ ] A prism for decomposition
1. [x] A microlens array
    > Correct: each microlens projects a sub-image onto a sensor area, thus encoding the different angular directions of light.
1. [ ] A binary mask


### Le mot "plénoptique" (plenoptic) vient de quelles origines etymologiques ?

> Pense au sens des racines latine et grecque qui composent ce mot.

1. [ ] Du latin plenus (plein) et du grec graphein (écrire)
1. [x] Du latin plenus (plein) et du grec optikos (qui concerne la vision)
    > Correct : plenus = plein, optikos = vision. Littéralement : "voir tout", ce qui résume bien l'objectif de capturer l'intégralité du champ lumineux.
1. [ ] Du grec plenios (lumière) et du latin optare (choisir)
1. [ ] Du latin plenus (plein) et du grec topos (lieu)

title: Computational Imaging — Quiz
text:
Level 2 — Comprehension

### Dans la pile focale (focal stack), pourquoi est-il necessaire d'aligner les images avant de les fusionner ?

> Pense a ce qui change optiquement quand on modifie la distance de mise au point.

1. [ ] Parce que la caméra bouge physiquement entre les prises.
1. [x] Parce que changer la distance de mise au point modifie la magnification, donc le champ de vue de chaque image est légèrement différent.
    > Correct : quand D' change, m = f / (D' - f) change aussi. Les images ont des tailles légèrement différentes et doivent être recalées avant fusion.
1. [ ] Parce que la luminosité varie entre les prises.
1. [ ] Parce que la couleur des pixels change avec la mise au point.


### Quelle operation mathematique est utilisee pour mesurer la nettete locale d'un pixel dans la pile focale ?

> Pense a l'opérateur qui réagit fortement aux contours et aux zones à haute fréquence spatiale.

1. [ ] La transformée de Fourier locale
1. [ ] La moyenne des pixels voisins
1. [x] L'opérateur Laplacien
    > Correct : le Laplacien mesure la variation locale d'intensité. Une zone nette produit une forte réponse Laplacienne (contours francs), une zone floue produit une réponse faible.
1. [ ] Le filtre médian


### Parmi ces affirmations sur le champ lumineux 4D, lesquelles sont correctes ?

> Rappelle-toi de la paramétrisation à deux plans et de ce qu'elle encode.

- [x] Un rayon est représenté par ses positions sur deux plans parallèles (plan st et plan uv).
    > Correct : c'est la paramétrisation à deux plans. Le plan st correspond typiquement à la lentille, le plan uv au capteur.
- [ ] Le champ lumineux 4D encode uniquement l'information de profondeur.
    > Incorrect : il encode à la fois l'information spatiale ET angulaire, ce qui permet la refocalisation, le changement de point de vue, etc.
- [x] Le même champ lumineux peut être capturé par une caméra plénoptique ou par une caméra sténopé déplacée vers plusieurs points de vue.
    > Correct : c'est un résultat fondamental — les deux approches mesurent le même ensemble de rayons.
- [ ] Le champ lumineux 4D est strictement nécessaire pour reconstruire une image 2D.
    > Incorrect : une image 2D ne nécessite qu'une projection du champ, pas sa capture complète.


### Quels sont les deux types de sortie produits par une caméra a ouverture codee a partir d'une seule image d'entree ?

> Pense aux deux informations complémentaires que l'on souhaite extraire d'une scène 3D.

- [x] Une carte de profondeur (Depth Map)
    > Correct : l'ouverture codée permet d'estimer la profondeur de chaque région de la scène depuis une seule image.
- [ ] Une sequence video reconstruite
- [x] Une image tout-net (All-Focused Image)
    > Correct : en combinant l'estimation de profondeur avec la déconvolution, on reconstruit une image où tous les plans sont nets.
- [ ] Un modele 3D de la scene


### Pourquoi la deconvolution est-elle un probleme "mal pose" (ill-posed) ?

> Pense à ce que signifie mathématiquement résoudre f convolué avec x = y pour trouver x.

1. [ ] Parce que le filtre f est toujours inconnu.
1. [ ] Parce que le capteur introduit du bruit.
1. [x] Parce que l'équation f convolué avec x = y admet en général plusieurs solutions x différentes qui sont toutes cohérentes avec l'observation y.
    > Correct : la convolution perd de l'information (notamment aux fréquences où le filtre s'annule). Plusieurs images nettes différentes peuvent donner la même image floue.
1. [ ] Parce que la convolution n'est pas une opération inversible dans le domaine spatial.


### Dans la deconvolution avec prior, que represente le terme lambda dans la formule d'optimisation ?

> Formule : x = argmin ||f x - y||^2 + lambda * somme rho(nabla xi)

1. [ ] La taille du noyau de flou.
1. [x] Le paramètre de régularisation qui contrôle l'équilibre entre fidélité aux données et respect du prior.
    > Correct : un lambda grand donne plus de poids au prior (image plus lisse, plus "naturelle"), un lambda petit donne plus de poids à la fidélité aux données observées.
1. [ ] L'inverse de la profondeur estimée.
1. [ ] Le nombre d'itérations de l'algorithme.


### Quel est l'avantage du prior epars (rho = norme gradient puissance 0.8) par rapport au prior gaussien (rho = norme gradient au carre) pour la deconvolution ?

> Pense à la distribution des gradients dans une image naturelle.

1. [ ] Il converge plus vite numériquement.
1. [ ] Il ne nécessite pas de connaitre le noyau de flou.
1. [x] Il préserve mieux les contours nets en localisant les gradients, plutôt que de les diffuser uniformément.
    > Correct : la norme puissance 0.8 est plus proche d'une norme L1 que L2 — elle favorise les solutions avec peu de gradients forts (contours) et de nombreuses zones uniformes, ce qui correspond aux images naturelles.
1. [ ] Il élimine totalement les artefacts de ringing.


### Pourquoi l'ouverture codee ameliore-t-elle la discrimination entre differentes profondeurs par rapport a une ouverture conventionnelle ?

> Pense à la structure visuelle du PSF dans chaque cas et à sa ressemblance avec des images naturelles.

1. [ ] Parce qu'elle rend le PSF plus petit, donc le flou est réduit.
1. [ ] Parce qu'elle augmente la quantité de lumière collectée.
1. [x] Parce que le PSF pseudo-aléatoire de l'ouverture codée est structurellement très différent des images naturelles, ce qui rend les profondeurs incorrectes facilement détectables.
    > Correct : avec une ouverture conventionnelle, le PSF ressemble à une tache lisse — difficile à distinguer d'une zone naturellement floue. Le PSF codé est si caractéristique qu'une mauvaise profondeur produit des artefacts clairement non-naturels.
1. [ ] Parce qu'elle génère un PSF invariant à la profondeur.

title: Computational Imaging — Quiz
text:
Level 3 — Mastery

### Remets les etapes de la fusion d'une pile focale dans le bon ordre.

> Pense au pipeline complet depuis les images brutes jusqu'à l'image tout-nette finale.

1. Capturer les images avec differentes mises au point
2. Aligner les images en corrigeant la magnification
3. Calculer les poids de nettete via le Laplacien
4. Lisser les cartes de poids par flou gaussien
5. Calculer la moyenne ponderee normalisee


### Un ingénieur capture une pile focale d'un objet de 10 cm de long en macrophotographie. Après fusion, il observe des halos (artefacts) aux bords des zones nettes. Quelle en est la cause la plus probable ?

> Pense aux étapes de traitement des poids dans la pile focale et à ce qui se passe aux transitions entre zones nettes et floues.

1. [x] Les poids Laplaciens n'ont pas été suffisamment lissés, créant des transitions abruptes entre zones de mise au point différentes.
    > Correct : sans lissage gaussien des poids, les frontières entre zones assignées à différentes images de la pile créent des discontinuités visibles (halos, bandes). Le flou gaussien sur les poids est crucial pour des transitions douces.
1. [ ] La bague de focus a été tournée trop rapidement entre les prises.
1. [ ] La résolution du capteur est insuffisante pour la macrophotographie.
1. [ ] L'alignement des images a été effectué avec une mauvaise valeur de focale.


### Dans une caméra plénoptique avec un capteur de N x N pixels et des microlentilles couvrant chacune k x k pixels, quelle est la résolution spatiale approximative de l'image finale reconstruite ?

> Pense au compromis fondamental introduit par le réseau de microlentilles.

1. [ ] N x N pixels (inchangé)
1. [ ] N/2 x N/2 pixels
1. [x] (N/k) x (N/k) pixels
    > Correct : chaque microlentille occupe k x k pixels du capteur pour encoder l'information angulaire. Il reste donc N/k microlentilles dans chaque direction, donnant une résolution spatiale de (N/k) x (N/k). C'est le compromis fondamental résolution spatiale / angulaire.
1. [ ] (N*k) x (N*k) pixels


### Remets les etapes de l'algorithme d'estimation de profondeur par ouverture codee dans le bon ordre.

> Pense à la logique de déconvolution à différentes échelles et à la sélection du meilleur résultat.

1. Selectionner une fenetre locale de l'image floue
2. Pour chaque profondeur candidate, deconvoluer avec le PSF calibre correspondant
3. Evaluer la qualite naturelle de chaque image deconvoluee (prior)
4. Retenir l'echelle dont le resultat est le plus naturel
5. Utiliser cette echelle comme estimation de profondeur et l'image correspondante comme image nette locale


### Un système de wavefront coding utilise une plaque de phase cubique. Quelle propriété clé du PSF résultant permet de simplifier le traitement par rapport à l'ouverture codée classique ?

> Compare le comportement du PSF en fonction de la profondeur dans les deux approches.

1. [ ] Le PSF est plus petit qu'avec une lentille conventionnelle.
1. [ ] Le PSF n'a pas de zéros dans son spectre fréquentiel.
1. [x] Le PSF est approximativement invariant à la profondeur, ce qui permet d'utiliser une seule déconvolution globale pour toute la scène.
    > Correct : c'est l'avantage clé du wavefront coding. Avec une ouverture codée classique, le PSF change de taille selon la profondeur et il faut une déconvolution locale par région. Ici, un seul PSF "fixe" est valable sur toute une plage de profondeurs.
1. [ ] Le PSF est une fonction gaussienne parfaite, facile à inverser.


### Pourquoi la technique de flux focal (focal flow) ne fonctionne-t-elle que sur les zones texturees ?

> Pense à ce qu'est le flux optique et aux conditions nécessaires pour l'estimer.

1. [ ] Parce que les zones lisses absorbent trop de lumière.
1. [ ] Parce que les microlentilles ne couvrent que les zones texturées.
1. [x] Parce que le flux optique ne peut être estimé que là où il existe un gradient d'intensité — les zones uniformes ne produisent pas de signal de flux exploitable.
    > Correct : le flux optique mesure le déplacement apparent de structures visuelles entre images. Sans texture (zone uniforme), il n'y a pas de structure à suivre, donc pas de flux mesurable, donc pas d'estimation de profondeur possible.
1. [ ] Parce que la convolution gaussienne efface les zones lisses.


### Quels enonces décrivent correctement l'ecart de dimensionnalite (dimensionality gap) introduit par Ng (2005) ?

> Pense aux dimensions du champ lumineux complet et à celles réellement utiles pour reconstruire image + profondeur.

- [x] Le champ lumineux complet est de dimension 4D.
    > Correct : avec la paramétrisation à deux plans, un rayon est décrit par 4 coordonnées (s, t, u, v).
- [x] Pour reconstruire une image plus sa carte de profondeur, seules 3 dimensions sont utiles : 2D image + 1D profondeur.
    > Correct : c'est la dimension utile — image 2D + profondeur 1D = 3D. Il y a donc 1 dimension "en trop" dans le champ lumineux complet.
- [ ] L'écart de dimensionnalité signifie que le champ lumineux est sous-échantillonné.
    > Incorrect : il ne s'agit pas d'un problème d'échantillonnage, mais d'un constat que le champ lumineux 4D contient plus d'information que ce qui est strictement nécessaire pour image + profondeur.
- [x] La lentille réseau exploite cet écart en ne capturant que le sous-ensemble de rayons correspondant à la variété 3D utile.
    > Correct : c'est précisément l'idée de la lentille réseau — capturer intelligemment uniquement la partie utile du champ lumineux 4D.


### Un chercheur dispose d'une seule image floue d'une scène et souhaite estimer la profondeur par ouverture codee. Il observe que deux échelles de PSF différentes produisent des images déconvoluées qui semblent toutes les deux naturelles. Quelle est l'explication la plus probable et la solution ?

> Pense aux conditions dans lesquelles l'ambiguïté d'échelle persiste malgré l'ouverture codée.

1. [ ] Le capteur est défectueux — il faut le remplacer.
1. [ ] L'ouverture codée est mal fabriquée — son motif est trop régulier.
1. [x] La région analysée est peu texturée ou homogène, ce qui rend tous les PSFs visuellement similaires dans cette zone — il faut soit utiliser une région plus texturée voisine, soit appliquer un prior plus fort.
    > Correct : même avec une ouverture codée, les régions peu texturées produisent des observations qui sont compatibles avec plusieurs profondeurs. La discrimination est plus facile sur les zones riches en hautes fréquences spatiales.
1. [ ] Le prior utilisé est trop fort — il écrase toutes les différences entre échelles.


### Quelles affirmations sur la comparaison entre les trois methodes de capture du champ lumineux sont correctes ?

> Compare reseau de cameras, camera unique deplacee et camera plenoptique selon plusieurs criteres.

- [x] Le réseau de caméras (Stanford Array) offre la meilleure qualité mais est coûteux et encombrant.
    > Correct : chaque caméra capture avec sa pleine résolution, mais l'installation est complexe et onéreuse.
- [x] La caméra unique déplacée ne peut capturer que des scènes statiques.
    > Correct : déplacer la caméra prend du temps — tout objet en mouvement dans la scène créera des incohérences entre les vues.
- [ ] La caméra plénoptique offre la même résolution spatiale qu'une caméra conventionnelle équivalente.
    > Incorrect : la résolution spatiale est réduite d'un facteur k (taille des microlentilles) car une partie des pixels est utilisée pour encoder l'information angulaire.
- [x] La caméra plénoptique est la seule des trois à capturer le champ lumineux en une seule prise instantanée.
    > Correct : c'est son avantage principal — elle permet de capturer des scènes dynamiques tout en préservant la capacité de refocalisation a posteriori.


### Parmi les techniques d'inférence de profondeur à partir de piles focales, laquelle nécessite le moins de captures et comment ?

> Compare les entrées requises par chaque technique : depth from defocus, depth from focus, confocal stereo, focal flow.

1. [ ] La pile focale standard (depth from focus), car elle utilise toutes les images.
1. [x] La profondeur depuis le défocus (depth from defocus), car elle ne nécessite que 2 images avec des niveaux de flou différents.
    > Correct : avec seulement 2 images g1 = f * h_sigma1 et g2 = f * h_sigma2, on peut estimer le paramètre sigma local (taille du flou) et en déduire la profondeur. Toutes les autres techniques nécessitent plus de captures.
1. [ ] Le stéréo confocal, car il combine focus et ouverture en une seule pile.
1. [ ] Le flux focal (focal flow), car il travaille uniquement sur des paires successives.
