title: Exam questions — Quiz
text:
Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging

### In a computational imaging system, what is the role of the optics?

> Think about the fundamental difference between traditional imaging and computational imaging.

1. [ ] Directly produce a recognizable, high-quality image
1. [x] Encode the scene information into an intermediate representation
    > Correct: optics encodes, computation decodes — the two are co-designed and inseparable.
1. [ ] Improve the captured image by removing noise
1. [ ] Compress the data to reduce bandwidth


### The inverse problem in computational imaging is written $y = Ax + n$. What does $A$ represent?

> Think about the components of the image formation model.

1. [ ] The unknown image to reconstruct
1. [ ] Measurement noise
1. [x] The measurement operator that encodes the physics of the system
    > Correct: $A$ encodes the system physics (optics, sensor). It links the scene $x$ to the measurements $y$.
1. [ ] The raw measurement vector


### Why does the inverse problem in computational imaging require regularization?

> Recall Hadamard’s conditions for a problem to be well-posed.

1. [ ] Because reconstruction algorithms are too slow without regularization
1. [ ] Because noise is always Gaussian
1. [ ] Because the operator $A$ is always diagonal
1. [x] Because the problem is often ill-posed: it may have neither a unique solution nor a stable solution
    > Correct: regularization introduces a prior on $x$ to constrain the solution space and stabilize reconstruction.


### Which statements correctly characterize computational imaging compared to traditional imaging?

> Think about the two fundamental steps: optical encoding and computational recovery.

- [x] The sensor and the algorithm are co-designed and inseparable
    > Correct: this is the deepest distinctive feature of the field.
- [ ] Computation only intervenes downstream to enhance an already recognizable image
    > Incorrect: that is the definition of traditional imaging.
- [x] The intermediate captured image is not necessarily recognizable to a human
    > Correct: the coded representation requires computation to be decoded.
- [x] The intersection of mathematics, physics, and computation is constitutive of the field
    > Correct: the three disciplinary pillars are inseparable.
- [ ] The optics can be modified independently of the reconstruction algorithm
    > Incorrect: any change in the optics implies adapting the algorithm.



Question 2 — Main topics

### Put the main topic families of the course in a logical order, from acquisition to display.

> Think of the full pipeline: from human perception to display, via capture and processing.

1. Human visual system
2. Digital photography
3. Computational photography
4. Deep learning and optimization
5. Compressive imaging
6. Wave optics and deep optics
7. Computational displays


### Which technique is associated with compressive imaging in the course?

> This domain exploits a mathematical property of natural signals to reduce the number of measurements.

1. [ ] Post-capture digital refocusing
1. [ ] Filtered back-projection reconstruction
1. [x] The single-pixel camera combined with successive random masks
    > Correct: it is the emblematic example of compressive imaging — a single photodiode reconstructs a 2D image thanks to signal sparsity.
1. [ ] Focal stacking for an all-in-focus image



Question 3 — Computational imaging in digital photography

### Smartphone night mode captures about 15 low-exposure images rather than a single long exposure. Why?

> Think about the main physical issue with a single long exposure.

1. [ ] To increase the spatial resolution of the final image
1. [x] To avoid motion blur while still accumulating enough light
    > Correct: each short image is sharp (no shake), and temporal fusion accumulates light as a long exposure would.
1. [ ] To reduce the sensor’s energy consumption
1. [ ] To capture several focus distances simultaneously


### Which computational photography techniques rely on capturing several successive images?

> Think of methods that cannot work with a single acquisition.

- [x] HDR (High Dynamic Range)
    > Correct: HDR merges several different exposures.
- [x] Night mode / burst photography
    > Correct: it merges about 15 aligned short exposures.
- [ ] Coded aperture
    > Incorrect: coded aperture extracts depth and an all-in-focus image from a single shot.
- [x] Focal stack
    > Correct: it captures a series of images at different focus distances.
- [ ] Hyperspectral imaging with a single filter
    > Incorrect: with the right sensor, this can acquire the spectrum in one shot.


### In smartphone computational photography, where does the photographic quality that exceeds the sensor’s optical limits mainly come from?

1. [ ] From a physically larger CMOS sensor
1. [ ] From high-precision lens optics
1. [x] From the power of processing algorithms that compensate for physical limitations
    > Correct: smartphones have small sensors and basic optics. Quality comes from computational processing, not optics.
1. [ ] From the high megapixel count



Question 4 — Computational imaging in medical imaging

### Which medical imaging modality acquires its data in Fourier space (k-space)?

> Think of the modality that exploits hydrogen spin precession.

1. [ ] Positron emission tomography (PET)
1. [ ] Ultrasound
1. [ ] X-ray radiography
1. [x] MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)
    > Correct: MRI measures in k-space and reconstructs the image via inverse Fourier transform.


### What is the fundamental common feature of ALL the medical imaging modalities mentioned in the course?

> Reflect on what makes medical imaging intrinsically computational.

1. [ ] They all use ionizing radiation
1. [ ] They all directly produce a 3D image without processing
1. [x] None directly produces a 3D image — all require algorithmic reconstruction
    > Correct: CT, PET, MRI, ultrasound — in all cases, 3D reconstruction is an inverse problem solved algorithmically.
1. [ ] They are all limited to anatomical imaging (not functional)


### Match each medical modality with its physical carrier and its type of information.

> Think about the physical interactions between radiation and biological tissue for each modality.

- [x] PET — radioactive tracers — functional and metabolic information
    > Correct: PET detects gamma photons emitted by positron annihilation from an injected tracer.
- [ ] MRI — X-rays — anatomical information
    > Incorrect: MRI uses magnetic resonance of hydrogen nuclei, not X-rays.
- [x] CT — multi-angle X-rays — slice image via back-projection
    > Correct: CT is radiography from multiple angles enabling volumetric reconstruction.
- [x] Ultrasound — high-frequency pressure waves — backscatter on tissue interfaces
    > Correct: ultrasound exploits reflection of ultrasound at biological interfaces.



Question 5 — Computational imaging in microscopy

### In classical optical microscopy, what is the resolution limit imposed by Abbe’s criterion?

> The formula involves wavelength and the objective’s numerical aperture.

1. [ ] About 20 micrometers for visible light
1. [x] About 200 nanometers for visible light
    > Correct: the limit is about $\lambda/(2\,NA)$, i.e. ~200 nm for visible light.
1. [ ] About 2 nanometers for visible light
1. [ ] About 2 millimeters for visible light


### Which nano-magnetic imaging technique offers the finest resolution among those presented in the course?

> Order them by decreasing resolution: MRFM, NV-NanoMRI, ESR-STM.

1. [ ] MRFM (~1 nm resolution, range ~100 nm)
1. [ ] NV-NanoMRI (~0.1 nm resolution, range ~10 nm)
1. [x] ESR-STM (resolution below 0.1 nm, range ~1 nm)
    > Correct: ESR-STM reaches sub-ångström resolution, the finest of the three techniques.


### Why is focal stacking indispensable in conventional optical microscopy?

1. [ ] Because microscope objectives have too large a numerical aperture
1. [ ] Because the sensor cannot record high spatial frequencies
1. [x] Because the depth of field of objectives is extremely small, on the order of a micrometer
    > Correct: with shallow depth of field, only a thin slice of the specimen is sharp — focal stacking fuses images at different focal planes into a fully sharp image.
1. [ ] Because biological samples move too fast



Question 6 — Computational imaging in astronomy

### The SKA (Square Kilometre Array) does not directly produce astronomical images. What does it produce as raw data?

> Think about the underlying interferometry technique.

1. [ ] Direct high-resolution photographs
1. [x] Visibilities, i.e., correlations between pairs of antennas
    > Correct: visibilities are the raw data. Algorithms (CLEAN, Bayesian methods) turn them into radio-astronomy images.
1. [ ] Brightness spectra integrated over the whole sky
1. [ ] Directly readable brightness temperature maps


### Approximately what compute power is required per SKA instrument?

> Order of magnitude to remember to illustrate the computational scale.

1. [ ] ~130 TFlops per instrument
1. [ ] ~130 GFlops per instrument
1. [x] ~130 PFlops per instrument
    > Correct: SKA needs about 130 petaFLOPS per instrument, illustrating the planetary scale of the challenge.
1. [ ] ~130 EFlops per instrument


### Astronomical long-baseline interferometric imaging (VLBI) simulates a telescope whose effective diameter equals what distance?

1. [ ] The diameter of each individual antenna
1. [ ] The average distance between antennas
1. [x] The distance between the farthest antennas in the array
    > Correct: this is aperture synthesis — the array simulates a single telescope whose diameter equals the largest baseline.
1. [ ] The wavelength of the observed radio signal



Question 7 — Deep optics

### In Deep Optics, what fundamentally distinguishes the training phase from the inference phase?

> Think about what is done in simulation versus what is deployed physically.

1. [ ] During training, only the network is optimized; during inference, only the optics is used
1. [x] During training, optics and network are co-optimized in simulation; during inference, the optimized lens is physically fabricated and the network deployed
    > Correct: training is fully digital (differentiable optics simulation + backprop). Inference involves physical fabrication of the lens.
1. [ ] During training, only the lens parameters are modified
1. [ ] There is no distinction — both phases are identical


### Why must the physical layer of a Deep Optics system be parameterized in a differentiable way?

> Think about what is required for end-to-end gradient-based optimization.

1. [ ] To enable lens fabrication by 3D printing
1. [ ] To make the optical system invariant to aberrations
1. [x] To allow the loss gradient to flow through the optics simulation back to the lens parameters
    > Correct: without differentiability, one cannot compute gradients with respect to lens geometry parameters, hence cannot optimize them.
1. [ ] To guarantee that the PSF is depth-invariant


### Deep optics challenges a fundamental principle of classical optical design. Which one?

1. [ ] The lens must be fabricated from high-purity glass
1. [x] The lens must produce a visually pleasing, recognizable image
    > Correct: in Deep Optics, a seemingly “defective” (highly aberrated) lens can outperform a perfect one if it encodes information more discriminatively for the target task.
1. [ ] The reconstruction algorithm must be linear
1. [ ] The PSF must be shift-invariant



Question 8 — NLOS imaging

### Which light bounce is exploited in NLOS imaging to localize a hidden object?

> Count the interactions: laser → wall → object → wall → sensor.

1. [ ] The first bounce (direct reflection on the wall)
1. [ ] The second bounce
1. [x] The third bounce
    > Correct: the path is laser → visible wall → hidden object → visible wall → sensor. The time difference with the direct path encodes position.
1. [ ] The fourth bounce or higher


### Which component of an NLOS setup measures photon arrival times with picosecond-scale precision?

> This detector can respond to a single photon.

1. [ ] A standard CMOS sensor
1. [ ] A standard photomultiplier (PMT)
1. [x] A SPAD sensor (Single-Photon Avalanche Diode)
    > Correct: a SPAD is a single-photon detector with tens-of-picoseconds time resolution, necessary to resolve path differences of a few centimeters.
1. [ ] A Michelson interferometer


### The useful signal (3rd bounce) in NLOS imaging is roughly how many times weaker than the direct signal?

1. [ ] 2 to 5 times weaker
1. [ ] 10,000 times weaker
1. [x] 10 to 100 times weaker
    > Correct: this is the main algorithmic challenge — extracting a weak signal buried in a much stronger background.
1. [ ] Same intensity as the direct signal



Question 9 — Parameters of HVS

### What is the angular resolution of normal visual acuity (20/20 notation)?

> It is the smallest angular separation the eye can resolve.

1. [ ] 1 degree
1. [ ] 1 arcsecond
1. [x] 1 arcminute
    > Correct: 20/20 corresponds to about 1 arcminute, i.e. the ability to distinguish two points ~1.5 mm apart at 5 meters.
1. [ ] 10 arcminutes


### What is the adapted dynamic range of the human visual system after full dark adaptation?

> Compare with instantaneous range (~5 orders) and current displays (~3 orders).

1. [ ] About 3 orders of magnitude (same as today’s displays)
1. [ ] About 6 orders of magnitude
1. [ ] About 20 orders of magnitude
1. [x] Up to 14 orders of magnitude (46.5 f-stops)
    > Correct: this superiority of the eye over sensors motivates HDR techniques in computational photography.


### The Contrast Sensitivity Function (CSF) of the human visual system drops at low spatial frequencies. What causes this drop?

1. [ ] The diffraction limit of the cornea
1. [ ] The finite size of photoreceptors
1. [x] Lateral inhibition in retinal ganglion cells
    > Correct: lateral inhibition (center-surround organization) penalizes very low frequencies, explaining the peak sensitivity around 4–6 cpd rather than at 0 cpd.
1. [ ] The insufficient number of rods in the fovea


### Put the peak-sensitivity wavelengths of the four photoreceptor types of the human eye in increasing order.

> From the shortest (blue) to the longest (red), passing through the rod peak.

1. S cones (blue) — 419 nm
2. Rods — 496 nm
3. M cones (green) — 531 nm
4. L cones (red) — 559 nm



Question 10 — Structure of the eye

### Which structure of the eye provides about 70% of total refraction and has a fixed curvature?

> Do not confuse it with the element that enables accommodation.

1. [ ] The crystalline lens
1. [ ] The vitreous humour
1. [x] The cornea
    > Correct: the cornea provides ~70% of refractive power but has a fixed curvature. The lens (~30%) adapts for accommodation.
1. [ ] The iris


### In near vision, how do the ciliary muscles and the zonular fibers act on the crystalline lens?

> The mechanism is counter-intuitive: muscle contraction → fiber relaxation.

1. [ ] Ciliary muscles relaxed → zonular fibers relaxed → lens flattens
1. [x] Ciliary muscles contracted → zonular fibers relaxed → lens becomes rounder (more convergent)
    > Correct: contracting the ciliary muscles reduces their diameter, which relaxes zonular tension, allowing the lens to take its naturally rounder shape.
1. [ ] Ciliary muscles contracted → zonular fibers taut → lens flattens
1. [ ] Ciliary muscles relaxed → zonular fibers taut → lens becomes rounder


### The optic disc (papilla) is the blind spot. Which anatomical property explains this?

1. [ ] Excessive rod concentration prevents signal transmission
1. [ ] The choroid absorbs all light at that point
1. [x] The optic disc contains no photoreceptors — it is the exit point of the optic nerve
    > Correct: ganglion-cell axons converge there to form the optic nerve, leaving no space for photoreceptors. The brain interpolates this gap.
1. [ ] The vitreous humour refracts light so that nothing is projected there



Question 11 — Structure and properties of retina

### The human retina contains approximately how many rods and cones?

> Remember the orders of magnitude — the difference is about a factor of 10.

1. [ ] ~10^6 rods and ~10^5 cones
1. [x] ~10^8 rods and ~10^7 cones
    > Correct: about 100 million rods and 10 million cones. Rods are 10× more numerous.
1. [ ] ~10^8 rods and ~10^8 cones (equal proportions)
1. [ ] ~10^5 rods and ~10^8 cones


### What is the consequence of strong rod convergence onto ganglion cells?

> Think about the fundamental trade-off between two antagonistic perceptual properties.

1. [ ] High spatial resolution but low light sensitivity
1. [x] High light sensitivity but low spatial resolution
    > Correct: many rods share a single ganglion cell, summing signals (gain in sensitivity) but losing precise location information (loss of resolution).
1. [ ] Good color vision but slow processing
1. [ ] Optimal vision in daylight but insensitivity to darkness


### Retinal ganglion cells (RGC) of type P and type M have different roles. Which pairing is correct?

1. [ ] M cells: color and spatial detail — P cells: motion and temporal resolution
1. [x] M cells: motion and temporal resolution — P cells: color and spatial detail
    > Correct: magnocellular (M) cells have strong convergence and specialize in motion; parvocellular (P) cells have weak convergence and encode color and fine detail.
1. [ ] Both types have identical functions and differ only in size
1. [ ] M cells: scotopic vision — P cells: photopic vision


### Why is night vision better when looking slightly to the side rather than directly?

> Think about the spatial distribution of rods on the retina.

1. [ ] Because the cornea refracts light better in peripheral vision
1. [ ] Because foveal cones are more sensitive than rods in low light
1. [x] Because rods are absent from the fovea and peak in density between 15 and 20 degrees of eccentricity
    > Correct: looking slightly aside projects a faint object onto rod-rich peripheral retina, much more sensitive than foveal cones under scotopic conditions.
1. [ ] Because the iris opens more in peripheral vision



Question 12 — Primary visual cortex

### What discovery did Hubel and Wiesel make in primary visual cortex (V1), rewarded by the 1981 Nobel Prize?

> These neurons are detectors of a very specific geometric property of the stimulus.

1. [ ] V1 neurons respond to specific color frequencies
1. [ ] V1 neurons directly encode object identity
1. [x] V1 neurons respond selectively to oriented edges at a specific orientation and position
    > Correct: V1 simple cells are oriented-edge detectors. Their discovery directly inspired filters learned in CNNs.
1. [ ] V1 neurons are organized into columns encoding only depth


### What is the functional difference between a V1 simple cell and a V1 complex cell?

> Position tolerance is the key criterion.

1. [ ] Simple cells respond to fast motion; complex cells to slow motion
1. [ ] Simple cells are color-sensitive; complex cells are achromatic
1. [x] Simple cells are selective to orientation AND a precise position; complex cells are orientation-selective but position-tolerant
    > Correct: a complex cell can be viewed as an aggregation of simple cells with the same preferred orientation, introducing local spatial invariance.
1. [ ] No functional difference — the distinction is purely morphological


### The dorsal stream and the ventral stream process two different kinds of information. Which ones?

> Memorize: ventral = “What”, dorsal = “Where”.

1. [ ] Ventral: motion — Dorsal: color
1. [x] Ventral: object recognition (the “What”) — Dorsal: localization and motion (the “Where”)
    > Correct: the ventral stream (V1→V4→IT) processes form, color, and identity. The dorsal stream (V1→MT→parietal) processes spatial location and motion.
1. [ ] Ventral: binocular vision — Dorsal: monocular vision
1. [ ] Ventral: low resolution — Dorsal: high resolution


### Put the stages of the visual pathway in order, from the retina to primary visual cortex.

> The visual signal passes through an intermediate thalamic relay before reaching cortex.

1. Retina (ganglion cells)
2. Optic nerve
3. Optic chiasm (partial decussation)
4. Lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)
5. Primary visual cortex (V1)



Question 13 — Network models

### Which computational model, proposed by Fukushima, is the direct precursor of convolutional neural networks (CNNs)?

> This model directly transposes the hierarchical V1 architecture discovered by Hubel and Wiesel.

1. [ ] Multilayer perceptron (MLP)
1. [ ] Hopfield network
1. [x] The Neocognitron
    > Correct: the Neocognitron alternates S layers (local filters, analogous to simple cells) and C layers (pooling, analogous to complex cells), achieving the first translation-invariant recognition in an artificial network.
1. [ ] Recurrent LSTM network


### In the LeNet architecture, pooling layers play a role analogous to which type of V1 cells?

> These cells tolerate small changes in stimulus position.

1. [ ] Center-surround cells
1. [ ] Simple cells
1. [x] Complex cells
    > Correct: spatial pooling introduces invariance to small translations — like V1 complex cells that activate for an orientation regardless of exact position.
1. [ ] P-type ganglion cells


### The selectivity of filters learned in early CNN layers resembles which V1 neuron type?

1. [ ] M-type ganglion cells
1. [ ] Ocular dominance neurons
1. [x] Simple cells — oriented Gabor-like filters
    > Correct: early CNN layers spontaneously learn Gabor-like filters (sine × Gaussian), mathematically close to V1 simple-cell responses.
1. [ ] Only parvocellular LGN neurons


### Are feedback connections (from higher areas back to V1) well modeled in current CNNs?

1. [ ] True — modern CNNs include explicit feedback connections inspired by the ventral stream
1. [x] False — the convolution + nonlinearity model does not capture these connections, which remain a recognized limitation
    > Correct: beyond V1, we still lack satisfactory computational models that include bidirectional connections. This is a major limitation of CNNs vs biological vision.



Question 14 — Conventional vs computational photography

### In a plenoptic camera, does the raw image captured by the sensor directly look like the photographed scene?

1. [ ] True — the plenoptic camera directly produces a refocused image
1. [x] False — the raw image is a set of angular footprints under the microlenses, not recognizable without a reconstruction algorithm
    > Correct: this is the emblematic example of computational photography — optics encodes, computation decodes. The raw image is not directly readable.


### What property characterizes a pinhole camera compared to a lens-based camera, and why does computational photography seek to combine their advantages?

> Think about the two antagonistic trade-offs: light efficiency vs depth of field.

1. [ ] The pinhole offers higher spatial resolution but reduced color sensitivity
1. [x] The pinhole offers infinite depth of field (everything sharp) but captures very little light, the opposite of a lens-based objective
    > Correct: computational photography aims to go beyond this trade-off — obtain sharpness across depth with good light efficiency.
1. [ ] The pinhole enables shorter exposures but with more geometric distortion
1. [ ] There is no significant difference between the two in terms of depth of field



Question 15 — Focal stack imaging

### Which mathematical operator is used to measure local sharpness in each image of a focal stack?

> This operator is sensitive to fast intensity variations — it detects edges.

1. [ ] The Fourier transform
1. [ ] The first-order gradient (Sobel operator)
1. [x] The Laplacian operator
    > Correct: the Laplacian responds strongly in sharp regions (well-defined edges) and near zero in blurred regions. It is then smoothed with a Gaussian filter.
1. [ ] Normalized cross-correlation


### Why must magnification be corrected between images of a focal stack before fusing them?

> Think about what happens to magnification when the lens–sensor distance $D'$ varies.

1. [ ] Because brightness changes with focus
1. [x] Because varying $D'$ changes magnification $m = f/(D'-f)$, which changes the image scale
    > Correct: when turning the focus ring, images do not have exactly the same magnification. Isotropic cropping/scaling is needed before fusion.
1. [ ] Because image color varies with focus
1. [ ] Because the field of view changes only in macro photography


### What extra information, in addition to an all-in-focus image, can be extracted from a focal stack?

> A pixel’s maximum sharpness in the stack is linked to a geometric property of the scene.

1. [ ] The spectral reflectance map of materials
1. [ ] The position of light sources in the scene
1. [x] The depth map — the focus setting where a pixel is sharpest reveals its distance to the camera
    > Correct: the depth of a scene point corresponds to the focus setting where it is sharpest in the stack. This is the principle of Depth from Focus.
1. [ ] The speed of moving objects in the scene



Question 16 — Depth inference

### The focal flow technique was inspired by the visual system of a particular animal. Which one?

> This animal has a secondary eye tube with two lenses that naturally create a focal-stack effect.

1. [ ] The mantis shrimp (*Odontodactylus scyllarus*)
1. [ ] The honey bee
1. [x] The jumping spider
    > Correct: the jumping spider has an eye tube with two retinal layers receiving different blur levels — it biologically performs what focal flow does numerically.
1. [ ] The pigeon


### Depth from Defocus requires how many input images?

> It is the most data-parsimonious technique among the four presented.

1. [ ] A single image
1. [x] Two images with different defocus levels
    > Correct: $g_1 = f * h_{\sigma_1}$ and $g_2 = f * h_{\sigma_2}$. Comparing the two allows estimating $\sigma$ (hence depth) without explicitly knowing $f$.
1. [ ] A full focal stack (10 images or more)
1. [ ] A stack combining focus AND variable aperture (2D stack)


### Which depth inference technique produces a per-pixel estimate (not per patch)?

> It is the most precise but also the most data-demanding.

1. [ ] Depth from Defocus
1. [ ] Depth from Focus
1. [ ] Focal flow
1. [x] Confocal stereo
    > Correct: confocal stereo uses a 2D stack (focus + aperture) and yields a per-pixel estimate — the finest granularity, at the cost of a much larger data volume.



Question 17 — Light field photography: principles

### The complete plenoptic function is 5D. Why can it be reduced to 4D to describe the light field in free space?

> Think about what is conserved along a light ray in the absence of scattering or absorption.

1. [ ] Because the human eye does not perceive the 5th dimension
1. [ ] Because modern sensors can only record 4 dimensions
1. [x] Because radiance is constant along a ray in free space, allowing a ray to be parameterized by its intersection with two planes
    > Correct: radiance conservation enables the two-plane parameterization $(s,t,u,v)$, reducing the description from 5D to 4D.
1. [ ] Because color is handled separately and is not part of the light field


### Which numerical operation on the light field simulates reducing the aperture after capture?

> Think about which pixels under each microlens correspond to rays passing through the aperture center.

1. [ ] Sum all sub-images from all microlenses without shifting
1. [x] Sum only the central pixels under each microlens
    > Correct: central pixels correspond to rays that went through the aperture center — exactly what a stopped-down diaphragm would pass. This increases depth of field.
1. [ ] Shift extraction windows in the opposite direction for each microlens
1. [ ] Apply a Gaussian filter to each microlens sub-image


### What is the fundamental and unavoidable trade-off of the plenoptic camera?

1. [ ] The plenoptic camera can only work in natural light
1. [x] The sensor’s total resolution is shared between spatial resolution and angular resolution
    > Correct: the more distinct angular directions you want, the fewer pixels per view you have. Effective spatial resolution is lower than a conventional camera with the same sensor.
1. [ ] Digital refocusing necessarily introduces motion blur
1. [ ] The plenoptic camera can capture only one focus setting per shot


### Who originated the concept of integral photography (ancestor of the plenoptic camera) and in what year?

1. [ ] Yann LeCun, in 1998
1. [ ] Ren Ng, in 2005
1. [ ] Ernst Abbe, in 1873
1. [x] Gabriel Lippmann, in 1908 (Scientific American article of Aug 19, 1911)
    > Correct: Lippmann conceptualized integral photography in 1908. Practical realization became possible only with modern digital sensors.



Question 18 — Light field: hardware particularities

### Which hardware approach for capturing the light field can handle dynamic scenes (moving objects)?

> The key constraint is to capture all views simultaneously.

1. [ ] A single camera moved on a motorized stage
1. [ ] A single camera with a motorized focus ring
1. [x] An array of multiple cameras (like the Stanford Camera Array)
    > Correct: all cameras in the array capture simultaneously, eliminating inter-view motion blur. The other approaches require a static scene or rely on a single shot (plenoptic).
1. [ ] All approaches are equivalent for dynamic scenes


### In a plenoptic camera, where is the microlens array (MLA) located relative to the main lens and the sensor?

> Its position distinguishes the plenoptic camera from the lattice lens (Question 20).

1. [ ] In front of the main lens
1. [ ] At the same plane as the main lens
1. [x] Between the main lens and the sensor, directly on the sensor surface
    > Correct: the MLA is placed between the lens and the sensor (or bonded directly onto the CMOS). It directs to each pixel light coming from a precise angular direction of the aperture.
1. [ ] Behind the sensor, in the electronic processing system


### In the Lytro camera, which component is responsible for light-field-specific processing?

> It is not the CMOS sensor nor the connectivity module.

1. [ ] The Marvell Avastar 88W8787 SoC
1. [ ] The lens array
1. [x] The Light Field Engine
    > Correct: the Light Field Engine is the dedicated signal processor for plenoptic processing. The Marvell SoC handles WiFi/Bluetooth connectivity.
1. [ ] The light field sensor alone



Question 19 — Coded apertures

### What is the main advantage of using a coded aperture (pseudo-random binary mask) rather than a standard circular aperture?

> Think about discriminating defocus blur from naturally uniform content.

1. [ ] The coded aperture lets in more light than the standard aperture
1. [ ] The coded aperture yields a higher-resolution image
1. [x] The PSF carries a characteristic signature of the mask, easy to identify and to distinguish from naturally smooth content
    > Correct: unlike a smooth circular PSF, the coded PSF is recognizable at any depth. The pattern scale reveals depth, and its presence distinguishes defocus from natural smoothness.
1. [ ] The coded aperture entirely eliminates the need for regularization


### In deconvolution with a sparse prior, which gradient exponent is better than the Gaussian prior (exponent 2)?

> An exponent below 1 favors solutions with gradients concentrated on a few pixels (sharp edges).

1. [ ] An exponent of 1.5 (semi-quadratic)
1. [ ] An exponent of 1.0 (L1 regularization)
1. [x] An exponent of 0.8 (hyper-Laplacian or sparse prior)
    > Correct: $\rho(\nabla x) = \|\nabla x\|^{0.8}$ favors gradient sparsity (flat regions + sharp edges), outperforming Richardson–Lucy and the Gaussian prior for natural-image deconvolution.
1. [ ] An exponent of 0.0 (L0 norm penalty)


### Why is combining a mask with zero frequencies AND a sparse prior the optimal solution for coded apertures?

> The two issues are depth discrimination and deconvolution stability.

1. [ ] Because zero frequencies speed up computation and the prior reduces quantization noise
1. [ ] Because a mask without zero frequencies is physically impossible to manufacture
1. [x] Because zeros improve depth discrimination, and the sparse prior guides reconstruction even when some frequencies are lost (spectral zeros)
    > Correct: they are complementary — the mask optimizes depth encoding, and the prior compensates for the impossibility of inverting spectral zeros.
1. [ ] Because the sparse prior can remove zero frequencies a posteriori



Question 20 — Generalized optics

### Wavefront Coding modifies a lens surface to introduce an aberration. What effect is sought on the PSF?

> The goal is that the PSF does not change (or changes little) with object distance.

1. [ ] Make the PSF point-like (ideally sharp) at all depths
1. [ ] Make the PSF vary distinctively with depth in order to estimate depth
1. [x] Make the PSF approximately depth-invariant, enabling a single global deconvolution
    > Correct: a depth-invariant PSF enables one global deconvolution that restores sharpness over the whole scene — at the cost of not producing a depth map.
1. [ ] Maximize SNR for very distant objects


### The lattice lens is placed in front of the main lens, unlike the plenoptic camera. What is the consequence for the PSF?

> Compare with Wavefront Coding where the PSF is invariant.

1. [ ] The PSF becomes depth-invariant, as in Wavefront Coding
1. [ ] The PSF is always point-like, regardless of depth
1. [x] The PSF varies with depth, enabling local depth estimation
    > Correct: each microlens in the lattice deflects rays differently depending on depth, creating a PSF characteristic of each distance — this is the cue that enables depth estimation.
1. [ ] The PSF becomes circular and uniform, as with a standard aperture


### What is the dimensionality gap introduced by Ng (2005) in relation to the lattice lens?

> The full light field is 4D. Which dimension corresponds to the information that is actually useful for image + depth?

1. [ ] The light field is 5D but only 2D are useful (the two spatial coordinates)
1. [ ] The full 4D light field is entirely necessary — there is no gap
1. [x] The light field is 4D but useful information (2D image + 1D depth) occupies only 3D — the lattice lens captures precisely this subspace
    > Correct: this dimensionality gap justifies the lattice lens as more efficient than capturing the full light field for image+depth applications.
1. [ ] The light field is 3D and the 4th dimension is always redundant


### Among the following systems, which one produces both a large depth of field AND a depth map from a single acquisition?

> Eliminate those that do not produce a depth map, and those that require multiple images.

1. [ ] Wavefront Coding
    > Incorrect: Wavefront Coding yields extended depth of field but no depth map (PSFs are identical).
1. [ ] Plenoptic camera
    > Incorrect: a plenoptic camera enables refocusing and depth estimation, but with reduced spatial resolution and without extended depth of field by default.
1. [x] Coded aperture
    > Correct: from a single image, coded aperture extracts an all-in-focus image and a (coarse) depth map.
1. [x] Lattice lens
    > Correct: the lattice lens yields a sharp image and depth from a single acquisition by exploiting PSF variation with depth.

PSF (Point Spread Function)

In-focus object → PSF = point
Out-of-focus object → PSF = blur with the shape of the aperture
Size of PSF ∝ distance to focal plane

Local convolution model:
\[y' = f_k \otimes x\]

\(y'\) = observed sub-window (blurred)
\(f_k\) = PSF calibrated at depth \(k\)

Challenge

title: Computational Imaging — Review
text:
Idea 1: Prior on natural images
Observation: natural images have sparse gradients.
Variational formulation:
\[x = \arg\min_x \; \underbrace{\|f \otimes x - y\|^2}_{\text{fidélité}} + \lambda \underbrace{\sum_i \rho(\nabla x_i)}_{\text{prior}}\]



Prior \(\rho\)
Effect




\(\|\nabla x\|^2\) (Gaussian)
Diffuse gradients → smooth


\(\|\nabla x\|^{0.8}\) (scattered)
Locates gradients → sharp edges









TipIntuition



The sparse prior selects the solution that most closely resembles a real natural image among all those that are consistent with the observation.

title: Computational Imaging — Review
text:
Idea 2: Coded Aperture
Principle: binary mask in the aperture plane → pseudo-random PSF, distinct from natural images.





flowchart LR
  A[Ouverture conventionnelle\nPSF ≈ naturel] -->|difficile à discriminer| B[Ambiguïté d'échelle]
  C[Ouverture codée\nPSF pseudo-aléatoire] -->|clairement non-naturel| D[Discrimination fiable]






Frequency domain:
\[\text{Convolution spatiale} \Leftrightarrow \text{Multiplication fréquentielle}\]
\[\hat{X} = \frac{\hat{Y}}{\hat{F}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{zéros de } \hat{F} \Rightarrow \text{division par zéro} \Rightarrow \text{ringing}\]








Configuration
+
-




Without spectral zeros
Easily reversible
Low discrimination


With spectral zeros
Better discrimination
Difficult inversion (→ prior)



Filter Design:

Criterion: maximize KL divergence between different depths
Constraints: physically feasible binary mask







WarningCritical point — Why “coded”?



Coded aperture reduces scale ambiguity. The correct depth is the only which gives a natural image after deconvolution. Bad ones produce clearly artificial artifacts.

title: Introduction to computational imaging
text:
Introduction to Computational Imaging

Why “imagery”?

Vision as the dominant sensory channel
Human beings are fundamentally a visual animal. Of all the senses, sight is by far the most used to acquire information about the world.
It is estimated that:

Approximately 75% of the information perceived by humans passes through the visual channel (sight)
Hearing only represents 13%
touch 6%, taste and smell approximately 3% each







TipIntuition



Designing systems that “see” the world effectively is therefore of paramount importance for interacting with the environment, whether robots, medical cameras or telescopes.


This observation explains why imaging — that is to say the formation, acquisition and interpretation of images — occupies a central place in computer science, physics and engineering.



Why “computational”?

Formal definition






NoteTo remember



Computational Imaging is the process of indirectly forming images from raw measurements, using algorithms that require a significant amount of computation.
Unlike traditional imaging, a computational imaging system involves tight integration between the acquisition system (the sensor) and the digital processing (the algorithm) to produce the desired images.




Fundamental difference with traditional imagery
The essential distinction lies in the role of calculation:
Traditional Imaging

Optics capture an image that directly resembles the real scene
The calculation improves this already recognizable image (deblurring, contrast improvement, etc.)

Pipeline: Real world → Optical → Captured image → Computing → Enhanced image
Computational Imaging

The optics encode the scene in an intermediate representation (often not directly recognizable)
The calculation decodes this representation to produce one or more final images

Pipeline: Real world → Generalized optics → Coded representation → Generalized computation → Final images






TipIntuition



In traditional imaging, the camera already does “all the optical work” and the computer does the fine-tuning. In computational imaging, the sensor and the algorithm are co-designed: one cannot work without the other.




The fundamental objective
The primary goal of computational imaging is to reconstruct human-recognizable images from measured data, relying on advanced algorithms. In traditional imaging, we rather seek to process already recognizable images to improve their quality or extract information from them.



What is computational imaging?

A revolution at the interface of physical and digital
The current revolution in capture techniques offers the possibility of accessing the physical world in unprecedented ways. But this revolution can only be achieved through skillful interaction between the physical world and the digital world.
Computational imaging advocates that, to develop effective imaging systems, it is necessary to move beyond the traditional decoupled pipeline — where sensor physics, image processing and the final application are considered separately.
Instead, we need to rethink imaging as an integrated model of acquisition and inference.


The three pillars of computational imaging
The domain is located at the intersection of three fields:

Mathematics: signal processing, optimization, machine learning
Physics: geometric optics, wave optics, electromagnetism
Calculation: reconstruction algorithms, artificial intelligence







NoteTo remember



Computational imaging belongs to both the physical/analog world (how light interacts with the sensor) and the digital world (how raw data is processed). This duality is its distinctive mark.




Optical layers
Optics can be modeled at different levels of detail:

Geometric Optics: light is treated like rays. This is the basic model for classic cameras and lenses. Unit: radiance (spectral). Properties: wavelength, polarization, direction.
Wave Optics: light is a wave. Diffraction and interference phenomena are taken into account. Necessary for systems with high resolution or operating near the diffraction limit.
Electromagnetism (E&M): the most general model. Applicable in extreme cases (nanometer, terahertz, etc.).







TipIntuition



For a standard smartphone camera, geometric optics are sufficient. For a super-resolution microscope or a hologram, wave optics is needed. For interactions on the atomic scale, complete electromagnetism is required.




The components of a computational imaging system
A complete system combines:

Optics (lenses, coded masks, mirrors, filters)
The sensor (CCD, CMOS, specialized detectors)
Calculation (reconstruction algorithms, neural network)

Two related approaches:

Computational imaging: optics + sensor + calculation → final image(s)
Computational Displays: calculation + optics + electronics → stimulation of the human visual system (the human is in the loop)



Two fundamental steps
Any computational imaging system is broken down into:

Optical Encoding: encode scene information optically using new optics, new sensors, new light sources
Computational Recovery: decode information using new algorithms




Biological example: the heart of computational imaging
Nature invented computational imaging long before humanity. The mantis shrimp (Odontodactylus scyllarus) has one of the most sophisticated visual systems in the animal kingdom.
Its compound eyes contain up to 16 types of photoreceptors (compared to 3 for humans), capable of perceiving the UV spectrum, circularly polarized light, and many other properties of light. This system “encodes” a phenomenal amount of optical information, and the animal’s brain “decodes” it to navigate, hunt and communicate.






TipIntuition



The mantis shrimp’s visual system is a perfect example of integration between sensor (the eyes) and computation (the brain): neither is useful alone. This is exactly the principle of computational imaging.




Modern areas of application
Computational imaging affects many sectors:

Digital photography (smartphones, reflex cameras)
Medical imaging (MRI, scanner, 3D ultrasound, PET)
Autonomous vehicles (LIDAR, cameras, radars)
Astronomy (radio telescopes, space telescopes)
Microscopy (nano-imaging, quantum imaging)
Industry (inspection, quality control)
Virtual and augmented reality (holographic displays)
Artistic analysis (X-ray fluorescence, multispectral imaging)

title: Introduction to computational imaging
text:
Motivating examples in computational imaging

Scale: from macro to micro
Computational imaging operates on an extraordinary range of scales, from cosmic structures to subatomic phenomena:



Object
Scale (meters)




Observable Universe
\(10^{26}\)


Galaxy
\(10^{19}\)


Solar system
\(10^{13}\)


Earth
\(10^7\)


Human
\(10^0\)


Cell
\(10^{-5}\)


Molecule
\(10^{-9}\)


Atom
\(10^{-12}\)


Atomic nucleus
\(10^{-14}\)


Planck scale
\(10^{-35}\)



This table illustrates the fundamental challenge: imaging systems must be adapted to each scale, because the physical principles (and therefore the algorithms) change radically from one order of magnitude to the next.


Microscopy at the nanoscale

Spin imaging by non-contact STM and AFM
Spin detection on the surface of materials with resolution at the atomic scale was achieved using two compatible methods:
Spin-Polarized Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (SP-STM)

Locally detects a spin component of the tunnel current
Allows you to visualize magnetic structures at the atomic scale
The measured current depends on the relative spin orientation of the tip and the sample

Non-Contact Atom Force Microscopy (nc-AFM)

Detects local forces linked to magnetic exchange
Sensitive to interactions between tip and surface spins
Complementary to SP-STM for complete characterization







TipIntuition



These techniques literally allow you to “see” how the spins are oriented on a surface, atom by atom. It is not an image in the photographic sense — it is a reconstruction from extremely weak electrical or mechanical signals.




Nanoscale magnetic resonance imaging
Magnetic Resonance Force Microscopy (MRFM)
MRFM uses mechanical force sensors to detect the weak magnetic signal from individual nuclear spins.
Three complementary approaches for nano-MRI:

MRFM: a nano-mechanical resonator associated with a nano-magnet generates a force on the spins of the sample. A microstrip acts as an antenna for the NMR spin inversion radio frequency pulses. Resolution range: ~1 nm, range ~100 nm.
NV-NanoMRI (Nitrogen Vacancy NanoMRI): an electronic spin defect in a diamond, located a few nanometers from the surface, serves as a magnetic sensor. Resolution ~0.1 nm, range ~10 nm.
ESR-STM (Electron Spin Resonance – Scanning Tunneling Microscopy): a tunneling current between the scanning tip and the conductive substrate constitutes the signal. Resolution < 0.1 nm, range ~1 nm.







NoteTo remember



These three techniques cover different resolution and range ranges, allowing magnetic characterization from the 100 nm scale to the atomic scale. In each case, the final image is algorithmically reconstructed from indirect signals — this is computational imaging par excellence.




Coherent X-ray magnetic imaging
Coherent X-ray Magnetic Imaging is a lensless approach to magnetic microscopy.
Its strong points:

Simultaneous access to phase contrast and absorption specific to chemical elements
Spatial resolution limited by wavelength: 5 nm in 2D and 10 nm in 3D

This technique has undergone remarkable development since 2004:

2004: Magnetic Fourier holography (Magnetic FTH)
2011: Magnetic Ptychography
2015: Monitoring the dynamics of skyrmions
2017: Mapping of spin textures in 3D
2021: Filming of spin dynamics on the femtosecond scale
2023: Capturing magnetic fluctuations
Future: Imaging at natural scales, widespread application







TipIntuition



A skyrmion is a swirling magnetic configuration, on the order of a few nanometers. Filming it in real time on the femtosecond scale (\(10^{-15}\) s) is a feat that is only possible thanks to the integration between a coherent X-ray source and advanced reconstruction algorithms.





Applications in astrophysics

The big questions of the Universe
Computational astrophysics seeks to answer some of the deepest questions:

What is dark matter and dark energy?
How were the first stars and galaxies formed?
Is the Universe alone home to life (SETI)?
How do gravitational waves confirm general relativity?
What is the large-scale structure of the Universe (filaments, cosmic voids)?

The standard cosmological model places the Big Bang 13.7 billion years ago. The first stars appeared ~400 million years later. Since then, the Universe has been in accelerated expansion under the effect of dark energy.


SKA: Square Kilometer Array
The Square Kilometer Array (SKA) is the largest radio telescope ever built, spread over two sites:
SKA1-Low (Western Australia, Murchison)

131,072 low frequency antennas (512 stations × 256 dipoles)
Frequencies: 50–350 MHz
Baselines: 65 km (11” resolution at 110 MHz)

SKA1-Mid (Karoo, South Africa)

197 parabolic antennas (133 × 15 m + 64 × 13.5 m MeerKAT)
Frequencies: 0.35–15.4 GHz
Baselines: 150 km (0.22” resolution at 1.7 GHz)

Scientific areas covered:

Tests of general relativity (extreme gravity, gravitational waves)
Cosmic dawn and reionization (first stars and galaxies)
Evolution of galaxies (z~2-3)
Cosmic magnetism (origin and evolution)
Cosmology (dark matter, large-scale structure)
Cradles of life (planets, molecules, SETI)



Colossal volume of data
The SKA generates an unprecedented data flow:

SKA1-Low: ~2 Pb/s at the antenna output, ~7 Tb/s after the central signal processor
SKA1-Mid: ~9 Tb/s at the antenna output, ~5 Tb/s after the central signal processor
Annual volume: ~300 PB/year per instrument
Computing power required: ~130 PFlops per instrument







WarningMassive computational challenge



The SKA will not directly produce astronomical images. It will produce visibilities (correlations between pairs of antennas). Transforming this raw data into astronomical radio images requires extremely powerful image reconstruction algorithms, running on dedicated supercomputers located in Perth and Cape Town. This is computational imaging on a planetary scale.





Medical imaging

Classification of medical imaging modalities
Medical imaging uses different information carriers to probe the human body in a non-invasive way:








Method
Information bearer
Type




Ultrasound (Ultrasound)
High frequency pressure waves
Backscatter/reflection


Radiography (X-ray)
Ionizing radiation
Transmission


Computed tomography (CT, C-arm)
Ionizing radiation
Transmission


Nuclear imaging (SPECT, PET)
Ionizing radiation
Broadcast


MRI (MRI)
Nuclear spin precession
Magnetic resonance



General medical imaging pipeline:

Acquisition of multiple 1D and 2D signals (projections, resonance signals, ultrasonic echoes)
Reconstruction of the 3D object from these signals







NoteTo remember



None of these modalities directly produces a 3D image. In all cases, the reconstruction of the three-dimensional object is an inverse problem solved algorithmically. Medical imaging is computational imaging.




Examples of medical images
Computed Tomography (CT)

Uses x-rays from multiple angles
Reconstruction by filtered back projection or iterative algorithms
Result: axial, coronal, sagittal sections, or 3D rendering of the skeleton and organs

Projected X-ray

2D image of X-ray transmission
Used for bones, lungs, joints

Positron Emission Tomography (PET)

Injection of a radioactive tracer (e.g. labeled glucose)
Detection of gamma photons emitted by annihilation of positrons
Reconstruction of metabolic distribution in the body

3D ultrasound (3D Ultrasound)

Mechanically or electronically scanned 2D image sequences
Volume reconstruction by interpolation
Widely used in obstetrics (fetal visualization)



Advanced MRI Modalities
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI / MRI) is available in several modalities:
Functional MRI (fMRI – Functional MRI)

Measures variations in blood oxygenation (BOLD signal)
Mapping of brain activity during cognitive tasks
Temporal resolution: a few seconds

Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA – MR Angiography)

Visualization of blood vessels without injection of contrast product
Detection of aneurysms, arterial stenoses

Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS)

Measures the chemical composition of tissues (metabolites)
Useful for tumor characterization

Current Density Imaging (CDI)

Reconstruction of the distribution of electrical currents in the brain or heart
Combines MRI and external electrical stimulation




Computational photography

Imaging by mobile devices
Modern smartphones incorporate sophisticated computational imaging systems. A high-end device may include:

Several lenses with different focal lengths (wide-angle, standard, telephoto)
A depth sensor (Time-of-Flight or stereo)
An infrared sensor for rapid focusing
A dedicated image processor (ISP) and neural chip







TipIntuition



The photographic quality of smartphones is not due to the size of their sensors (very small) nor to their optics (very basic), but to the power of the processing algorithms which combine several images to synthesize one of superior quality.




Advanced digital photography
HDR+ (High Dynamic Range Plus)

Captures multiple exposures in ultra-fast burst
Blending exposures to recover both highlights and shadows
Adaptive blending algorithm based on frame alignment

Night Mode

Captures a long sequence of images at low exposure
Sub-pixel alignment to correct micro-shake
Temporal fusion to accumulate light without motion blur







NoteTo remember



Google Night Mode (Night Sight) is an iconic example: it does not capture a single long exposure, but combines ~15 images taken in ~1 second. The result is a sharp, bright, low-noise image — impossible with a single capture. This is pure computational imaging.




Multi-sensor and hyperspectral imaging
Multi-sensor cameras (like the Light L16 with 16 lenses) allow:

Simultaneous capture from different focal lengths and angles
Super-resolution by merging images
Synthetic bokeh (background blur controllable after shooting)
Variable depth of field in post-processing

Hyperspectral imaging goes further by capturing dozens to hundreds of spectral bands, allowing the identification of materials, vegetation, pollutants, etc.



Automotive industry: autonomous vehicles

Multi-sensory modality
An autonomous vehicle is a multi-modal computational imaging system par excellence. It combines:

Cameras: detection and tracking of pedestrians, cyclists, traffic lights, open spaces and other elements of the road scene
LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging): high-precision laser sensors detecting fixed and moving objects, providing a dense 3D point cloud
Long-Range Radars: detection of vehicles and measurement of their speed over large distances
Articulating Radars: detection of moving vehicles over a wide field of vision
Short-Range Radars: detection of obstacles close to the vehicle



3D LiDAR for perception
LiDAR (e.g. Velodyne VLS-128) is one of the key sensors for autonomous vehicles:

Emits laser pulses in all directions
Measures the return time of each pulse (Time-of-Flight)
Reconstructs a 3D point cloud of the environment in real time
Typical range: 100–200 m, accuracy: a few centimeters







TipIntuition



LiDAR does not see an image in the photographic sense. It measures flight times of light pulses and deduces distances. La transformation de ces mesures en une représentation 3D utilisable est un problème d’imagerie computationnelle.





Solutions based on artificial intelligence

Deep Optics
Deep Optics is an approach that jointly optimizes physical optics and digital processing in an end-to-end manner.
Principles:
The system is divided into two layers:

Physical Layer: the lens or another optical component (coded mask, diffraction grating, etc.)
Digital Layer: a processing neural network

Training phase:

Optimization is done end-to-end in simulation
The gradient of the loss function is propagated through the digital layer and through the simulation of the optical component
Optics and network are co-optimized simultaneously

Inference phase:

The optimized lens (or other component) is physically manufactured
The trained network is deployed
Both layers work together to solve the target task

Possible interpretations:

The system can be seen as an optical encoder + electronic decoder
Or like a hybrid optical-electronic neural network, where the physical layer plays the role of the first layers of the network







NoteTo remember



Deep optics blurs the line between optical design and machine learning. Instead of designing the optics separately and then learning a processing algorithm, we optimize both simultaneously for the final task (e.g. object recognition, 3D reconstruction).





Analysis of works of art

Examine old paintings
Computational imaging offers non-invasive tools to study paintings without damaging them.
Structure of a painting (stratigraphy)
An old painting is made up of several superimposed layers (from bottom to top):

Canvas: the canvas or the wooden panel
Ground Layer (preparation layer): white coating (gesso)
Underdrawing (preparatory drawing): drawn with chalk, charcoal or ink
Imprimatura: thin layer of colored paint
Paint Layers: successive application of colors
Varnish/Glazes: protective varnish and transparent glazes

Each layer provides historical and artistic information. The objective is to image them separately without touching the work.


Traditional non-invasive imaging
Several classic imaging techniques make it possible to probe different layers:







Technical
What it reveals




Infrared (IR)
Preparatory drawing under the coat of paint


Visible
Painting as we see it


Ultraviolet (UV)
Restorations, varnishes and retouches


X-rays
The base layer (lead white), the pentiments, the structure of the canvas









TipIntuition



A painting can hide entire works beneath its surface. X-ray imaging revealed that some Picassos were hiding earlier compositions repainted by the artist. IR imaging has uncovered studies and compositional changes in da Vinci’s works.




Macro X-ray fluorescence (MA-XRF)
Physical principle of MA-XRF (Macro X-ray Fluorescence)

A primary X-ray beam hits the paint surface
The beam ejects an electron from an inner shell of an atom (photoelectric effect)
An electron from an outer shell fills the gap
This transition releases an X-ray fluorescence photon of energy characteristic of the chemical element
These photons are detected by an energy-selective detector

The MA-XRF datacube
MA-XRF produces volumetric data:

Spatial dimensions X and Y: position on the table (typically 1 to 100 million pixels)
Z dimension (energy): X spectrum between 0 and 40 keV, sampled on 4096 channels

Each pixel in the table has a MA-XRF spectrum: the location of the peaks in this spectrum identifies the chemical elements present (calcium, lead, mercury, copper, zinc, iron, manganese, etc.).
Extraction of elemental cards
From the datacube, we can extract a distribution map for each chemical element present in the paint.
Example on Goya (Dona Isabel de Porcel, NG1473, before 1805):

The RGB image shows the portrait of a woman
X-ray image reveals another male figure hidden underneath

Extraction of elemental cards:

Calcium → preparation layer (gesso)
Manganese → brown pigments (umbra)
Iron → ocher and red pigments
Mercury → vermilion (red HgS)
Lead → lead white (light background and highlights)
Copper → copper green or azurite (blues and greens)

Example on Van Gogh (The Sunflowers):
The deconvolution algorithm applied to the datacube reveals the spatial distribution of copper, zinc, iron and lead in the composition — allowing precise identification of the pigments used and their arrangement.


Machine learning extraction
MA-XRF also allows, combined with ML, to separate superimposed layers of paint.
Model used: the system takes the RGB image and the X-ray image as input, then predicts two separate images:

\(\hat{x}_1\): visible paint (surface)
\(\hat{x}_2\): the hidden (underlying) painting

Results on Goya:

Input 1: portrait of a woman (RGB)
Input 2: imprint of two superimposed faces (X-ray)
Output 1: woman’s face (isolated)
Output 2: face of the hidden man (isolated)







NoteTo remember



Separating paint layers using ML is an unsupervised inverse imaging problem: there is no “ground truth” to train the model. Specialized architectures (physical constraints, regularization) are necessary.





Imaging outside line of sight (NLOS)

Problem definition
Non-Line-Of-Sight Imaging (NLOS) is one of the most fascinating and counterintuitive problems in computational imaging.
Question: Is it possible to form an image of an object that we cannot see directly because it is hidden behind an obstacle?
Computational answer: Yes, by exploiting light bounces on diffuse surfaces.


Physical principle
Light does not only propagate in a straight line: it diffuses on surfaces. A white surface (a wall) re-emits light in all directions. If a hidden object illuminates a visible wall, the wall bears subtle traces of that object.
Experimental device:

Picosecond laser: emits ultra-short light pulses (duration ~ps = \(10^{-12}\) s)
2-axis galvanometric mirror: directs the laser towards different points on the wall
Beam splitter: separates the transmitted beam from the return signal
SPAD sensor (Single-Photon Avalanche Diode): single photon detector, ultra-sensitive and temporally resolved
Hidden: hides the object to be imaged

Measuring principle:

The laser illuminates a point P on the wall
Light scatters in all directions from P
A fraction reaches the hidden object, which in turn backscatters it
A fraction of this backscattered light returns to the wall, then to the sensor
The sensor measures the arrival time of each photon with a precision of the order of a few tens of picoseconds

Temporal explanation:
The difference between the first bounce (direct: laser → wall → sensor) and the third bounce (laser → wall → object → wall → sensor) encodes the position of the object.
Example :

1st bounce: 2.7 ns (40 cm additional travel)
3rd bounce: 4.3 ns
Difference: 4.3 - 2.7 = 1.6 ns → corresponds to ~24 cm of additional travel



Raw data and reconstruction
Raw measurements:
The acquired data forms a 3D volume of dimensions (x’, y’, t):

x’ and y’: position of the illumination point on the wall
t: flight time

This data is visualized as a Maximum Intensity Projection — it doesn’t look at all like the hidden object.
Reconstruction:
From these temporally resolved measurements, an algorithm (based on filtered back-projection or inverse optimization methods) reconstructs the 3D volume of the hidden object.
Experimental results (University of Geneva):

Hidden scene: a statue (discobolus) and a flowerpot behind a concealer
Measurements: noisy time-resolution volume, without visible structure
3D reconstruction: the two objects are clearly identifiable in the reconstructed volume







WarningAlgorithmic challenge



NLOS reconstruction is a severely underdetermined and noisy inverse problem. The signal of the 3rd bounce is 10 to 100 times weaker than that of the 1st bounce. Fast deconvolution algorithms (e.g. Phasor Fields algorithm) or compressed sensing type are necessary to obtain a usable reconstruction.


Potential applications:

Autonomous driving assistance (seeing on a street corner)
Rescue operations (locate people in a room without entering it)
Endoscopic medical imaging (see behind tissue folds)
Space missions

title: Introduction to computational imaging
text:
Main topics of the course

Human Visual System
The course includes a study of the human visual system, because understanding how the eye and brain process visual information is fundamental to designing effective imaging systems.
Topics covered:

Anatomy of the eye: cornea, lens, retina, photoreceptors (rods and cones)
Visual acuity, color and 3D vision: how do we discriminate details? How do we perceive colors and depth?
Contrast sensitivity (Contrast Sensitivity Function): what spatial frequencies does the eye perceive best?
Conflicts in Displays: Why can VR/AR displays cause nausea? How do perceptual boundaries guide design?
Refractive Errors: myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism — and how imaging systems can compensate for them

The human visual system can itself be modeled as a computational imaging system: sensors (photoreceptors) → network (optic nerve, lateral geniculate body) → computation (visual cortex).


Digital Photography
This module explores the foundations of digital photography:

Optics: image formation, aberrations, lenses
Aperture (Aperture): relationship between aperture, depth of field and quantity of light
Depth of Field: which objects are in focus? How to control it?
Field of View: relationship between focal length and angle of view
Exposure: compromise between exposure time, aperture and ISO
Noise: photon noise (shot noise), thermal noise, reading noise
Color Filter Arrays: Bayer mosaic — how does a monochrome sensor capture color?
Image processing pipeline (Image Processing Pipeline): demosaicing, white balance, gamma correction, compression



Computational Photography
Beyond classic digital photography, computational photography uses calculation to go further:

High Dynamic Range Imaging (HDR – High Dynamic Range Imaging): capture scenes with strong light contrasts
Tone Mapping: compression of an HDR image for display on a standard screen
Burst Photography & Night Sight: fusion of multiple images to improve quality
Coded Apertures: modify the point spread function (PSF) to encode depth or facilitate deconvolution
And many other techniques (super-resolution, focus stacking, panoramas, etc.)



Deep Learning for Computational Imaging
Deep learning has revolutionized computational imaging. This module covers:

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN): fundamentals, convolution layers, pooling, activation
DnCNN (Denoising CNN): deep architecture for image denoising
U-Net: encoder-decoder architecture with jump connections, used extensively in medical imaging and reconstruction
And other advanced architectures (transformers, diffusion models, etc.)



Optimization and deep learning
Solving inverse problems in imaging requires optimization tools:

Proximal Gradient Methods: iterative algorithms to minimize non-smooth functions (e.g. ISTA, FISTA)
Iterative Optimization with Deep Priors (Iterative Optimization with Deep Priors): incorporate the a priori knowledge learned by a neural network into an optimization loop
Resolution of general inverse problems in imaging: unified formulation of reconstruction problems







NoteTo remember



An inverse problem in imaging is typically written: \(y = Ax + n\), where \(y\) are the measurements, \(A\) is the measurement operator (the physics of the system), \(x\) is the unknown image and \(n\) is the noise. Finding \(x\) from \(y\) is often poorly posed and requires regularization (a priori on \(x\)).




Compressive Imaging
Compressive imaging (Compressed Sensing) exploits the parsimony of natural signals to drastically reduce the number of necessary measurements.
Applications:

Single-Pixel Camera: a single photodiode + successive random masks → reconstruction of a 2D image
Compressive Hyperspectral Imaging (Compressive Hyperspectral Imaging): acquisition of spectral datacubes with a reduced number of measurements
Compressive Light Field Imaging: captures the direction of light with fewer pixels

These techniques make it possible to design sensors that are less expensive, faster or operating in regimes where conventional sensors are difficult to manufacture (infrared, terahertz).


Introduction to wave optics and deep optics
This module delves deeper into wave phenomena and their applications:

Diffraction and interference (Diffraction & Interference): wave behavior of light
The diffraction limit (The Diffraction Limit): theoretical maximum resolution of an optical system
End-to-end optimization of optics and image processing: optical-algorithmic co-design (Deep Optics)
Phase Retrieval: reconstruct the amplitude and phase of a wavefield from intensity measurements only
Computer-Generated Holography: calculation of holograms for 3D displays



Computational Displays
The display is the symmetrical side of the acquisition. This module explores:

Gaze-Contingent Focus Displays: the focus dynamically changes depending on where the user is looking (Konrad et al., SIGCHI 2016; Padmanaban et al., PNAS 2017)
Near-Eye Light Field Displays: reproduction of the 4D light field in front of the eye for more comfortable virtual reality experiences (Huang et al., SIGGRAPH 2015; Wetzstein et al., SIGGRAPH 2011-2012)
Holographic Displays: reproduction of a complete wavefield (amplitude and phase) for a truly convincing 3D experience (Padmanaban et al., SIGGRAPH Asia 2019; Peng et al., SIGGRAPH Asia 2020; Choi et al., Optica 2021)

```{quizdown}
### Quel pourcentage de l'information humaine est acquis par le canal visuel ?

> Ce chiffre justifie l'importance centrale de l'imagerie.

1. [ ] 13 %
1. [ ] 50 %
1. [ ] 60 %
1. [x] 75 %

    > Correct : environ 75 % de l'information percue par l'etre humain transite par la vue, contre 13 % pour l'ouie.

### Quels sont les trois piliers de l'imagerie computationnelle ?

> Le domaine se situe a l'intersection de plusieurs disciplines.

- [x] Mathematiques

    > Correct : optimisation, traitement du signal et apprentissage automatique font partie des mathematiques appliquees a ce domaine.

- [x] Physique

    > Correct : l'optique geometrique, ondulatoire et l'electromagnetisme sont essentiels.

- [x] Calcul (Computation)

    > Correct : les algorithmes de reconstruction et l'intelligence artificielle constituent le troisieme pilier.

- [ ] Chimie

    > Incorrect : la chimie n'est pas l'un des trois piliers fondamentaux de l'imagerie computationnelle.

- [ ] Biologie

    > Incorrect : la biologie n'est pas un pilier fondamental, meme si certaines applications concernent le vivant.


### Quel modele optique traite la lumiere comme des rayons et est adapte aux cameras classiques ?

1. [ ] Optique ondulatoire (Wave Optics)
1. [ ] Electromagnetisme (E&M)
1. [ ] Optique diffractive (Diffractive Optics)



### Quelles affirmations decrivent correctement le pipeline de l'imagerie computationnelle ?

> Compare avec le pipeline de l'imagerie traditionnelle.

- [x] L'optique encode la scene dans une representation intermediaire

    > Correct : c'est la premiere etape du pipeline computationnel.

- [x] Le calcul decode la representation pour produire des images finales

    > Correct : c'est la deuxieme etape, inseparable de la premiere.

- [ ] L'image capturee est directement reconnaissable

    > Incorrect : c'est le cas de l'imagerie traditionnelle, pas computationnelle.

- [ ] Le calcul se limite a ameliorer une image deja formee

    > Incorrect : ameliorer une image existante est le role du calcul en imagerie traditionnelle.

    > Correct : ses 16 types de photorécepteurs encodent une representation riche, et son cerveau decode cette information. Capteur et calcul sont co-conçus.

    > Incorrect : les capteurs SPAD sont precisement choisis pour leur resolution temporelle au niveau de la picoseconde.

> Pense a ce qui est optimise et comment.

1. [ ] On entraine d'abord le reseau de neurones, puis on conçoit l'optique separement
1. [ ] On remplace l'optique physique par un reseau de neurones entierement numerique
1. [x] On co-optimise la couche physique (optique) et la couche numerique (reseau) de maniere bout-en-bout en simulation
    > Correct : le gradient de la fonction de perte se propage a travers le reseau ET a travers la simulation du composant optique.

1. [ ] Echographie 3D
1. [ ] CT scan

    > Correct : le PET utilise un traceur radioactif (souvent du glucose marque au F-18) dont les positrons emis permettent de localiser les zones metaboliquement actives.

    > Correct : un interferometre radio mesure des correlations dans le domaine de Fourier (plan uv). La transformation en image necessite une reconstruction inverse.
